Principles advise; controls enforce. Halt for human approval before violating a critical principle or performing a destructive, irreversible action.

# Category: architecture

## Gall's Law
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/architecture/gall-law
- Category: architecture · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: A complex system that works evolved from a simple system that worked — design for growth, not for the final vision.
> Ship the simplest system that works end-to-end, then grow it under real usage. Never plan a greenfield build as a single big-bang delivery of the final architecture — plan it as a sequence of working systems. When a design cannot be reached incrementally, treat that as a design flaw, not a scheduling problem.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Complex systems that work are invariably evolved from simple systems that worked; complex systems designed from scratch cannot be debugged into working, because you cannot debug something that has never run. The design task is therefore not to specify the final system but to specify the next small working system and the growth path between the steps. Ambition is allowed; big-bang delivery of ambition is not.

## When to use

- Greenfield products and platforms where requirements are still hypotheses.
- Migrations and rewrites — plan them as staged, strangler-style steps with running value at each stage.
- Architecture roadmaps: each phase must work, not merely assemble toward the end state.
- Anything where real usage patterns are unknown until users arrive.

## When NOT to use

- Re-implementing a proven, fully specified system — the final design is genuinely known; treat it as engineering, not exploration.
- Contractual or regulated deliverables that fix scope up front; deliver the simple core plus the mandatory control planes, not speculative features.
- Small utilities that are already the simple system — no evolution needed.
- Not an excuse to skip hard-to-reverse thinking: data models, security boundaries, and service seams deserve up-front care even while everything else stays simple.

## Anti-pattern

- A 200-page spec, a one-year build, and a launch date where the system runs for the first time.
- Building "the platform" before the first product that would run on it.
- Abstractions for imagined future scale — multi-region, multi-tenant, plugin systems with no plugins.
- Freezing a failed first version because "we already designed it" instead of evolving it.

## Code example

Wrong — the enterprise scaffold that must be completed before anything works:

```ts
// 14 packages, 0 served requests: EventBus, TenantResolver, RegionRouter...
export class EnterprisePlatform {
  async start() { /* still wiring — no behavior exists to test against */ }
}
```

Right — one vertical slice that works, plus a stated growth path:

```ts
// day 1: a request goes through; the team learns from real traffic
export async function signup(req: Request) {
  const user = await db.users.insert(parseSignup(req));
  await mailer.send(welcome(user));
}
// Growth path: extract the mailer behind a port when a second sender appears;
// shard db.users when measured load demands it — not before.
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced by process gates, not by intent:

- **Milestone gates**: no increment counts as done without a demo running end-to-end in a production-like environment.
- **WIP limits**: cap concurrent unfinished layers — an ever-growing unfinished platform is the signature failure this law warns about.
- **RFC discipline**: every proposal must answer "what is the smallest version that runs?" and "what will we learn from it?".
- **Metrics before scale**: dashboards and load data are prerequisites for approving the next complexity step.

## Real-world case

A company funded a one-year, 200-page-spec "enterprise platform": shared auth, workflow engine, reporting framework, and only then the first business module. Integration testing started at month ten and found the layers did not fit, while requirements had drifted for a year without feedback. The project was cancelled before serving a single customer. A rival internal team shipped a crude single-purpose service in six weeks, learned from real users, and quietly absorbed the business need. (ilustratif — composite of a common failure mode; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Evolution vs. up-front design**: some decisions (data model, security boundaries, service seams) are expensive to reverse — invest in those early even while everything else stays simple; see Chesterton's Fence for what already exists.
- **Growth path vs. YAGNI**: YAGNI says do not build the future; this law says plan the path to it. The compromise: build only the current working system, but avoid decisions that block the next one.
- **Simple-first vs. safety obligations**: "start simple" never starts unsafe — auth, backups, and least-authority must exist in version one, simple but present.

## Related principles

- [Conway's Law](/docs/principles/architecture/conways-law) — the org must be able to evolve with the system, or it will not.
- [KISS](/docs/principles/design/kiss) — the starting system should be simple, not merely small.
- [YAGNI](/docs/principles/design/yagni) — the counterweight to speculative platform layers.
- [Expand-Contract](/docs/principles/data/expand-contract) — the safe step size for schema evolution.
- [Observability-First](/docs/principles/reliability/observability-first) — you cannot evolve what you cannot see.
- [Chesterton's Fence](/docs/principles/design/chesterton-fence) — before removing inherited behavior, learn why it exists.

## References

- John Gall, *Systemantics: How Systems Really Work and How They Fail* — origin of the law (verification: perlu — confirm edition and exact wording before quoting).
- Google SRE Book — incremental rollout as the operational cousin of evolutionary design: https://sre.google/sre-book/ (verification: perlu for chapter-level claims).

## Conway's Law
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/architecture/conways-law
- Category: architecture · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Your architecture will mirror your team's communication structure — design the org, or it designs the system for you.
> Treat team structure and communication paths as first-class inputs to every architecture decision. When proposing service boundaries, first map who owns what and who actually talks to whom — the design will converge to that map whether you plan it or not. If the target architecture requires collaboration patterns the org does not have, either change the org or change the target.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

Organizations design systems that mirror their communication structures: the interfaces between modules will look like the lines between the people who built them. Conway stated it in 1967 as an observation about design committees — a design organization's outputs reflect its internal communication patterns. The engineering consequence is that org design is architecture design; if you cannot change the software, look at the communication paths that produced it.

## When to use

- Decomposing a monolith or defining service boundaries.
- Planning team topologies and ownership before, or together with, the architecture.
- Explaining why "the same broken shared thing" keeps reappearing after every rewrite.
- Mergers and reorgs: expect the architecture to drift toward the new org chart.

## When NOT to use

- Small teams where communication is already cheap — do not split one team into microservices to imitate a target org.
- Domains where the correct boundary genuinely cuts across existing team lines — pick the domain, then negotiate the org move (the "inverse Conway maneuver"), knowing it is slow.
- Compliance-mandated separation of duties: that org shape is a requirement, not a design smell to engineer around.

## Anti-pattern

- One "shared" service that four teams bolt their modules into, each breaking the others' assumptions.
- Architecture designed by a central committee with no delivery power — the shipped system follows the delivery teams' lines instead.
- Services split by technical layer (a frontend team, a database team) rather than by domain change.
- A "platform team" that owns everything other teams touch, becoming a serialization point for every feature.

## Code example

Wrong — one shared service mirrors a broken communication pattern:

```text
services/shared-core/
  billing.ts    # edited by the Payments team
  search.ts     # edited by the Search team
  reports.ts    # edited by whoever needed a chart that week
# one deployable, four review queues: every release waits on everyone
```

Right — ownership boundaries make the org chart explicit and cheap:

```yaml
# CODEOWNERS — the org chart becomes the boundary
/billing/**   @org/payments
/search/**    @org/search
/reports/**   @org/analytics
# each team ships its own service; cross-team talk goes through contracts
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced by ownership mechanics, not by org charts on slides:

- **CODEOWNERS**: required reviews per path — a PR touching two teams' modules is an automatic signal to extract a boundary.
- **Import boundary rules in CI** (dependency-cruiser, eslint-plugin-boundaries) that match the ownership map, not just folder aesthetics.
- **Service catalog metadata**: every service records its owning team; orphaned services fail audits.
- **Contract review process**: cross-team interfaces (APIs, events, shared schemas) require both owners' sign-off before merge.

## Real-world case

Four teams — payments, search, reports, and mobile — shared one "shared-core" service "to avoid duplication". Each bolted its own module in: payment batch jobs next to search indexing next to report queries, with no owner of the whole. Deploys became four-way negotiation, and each team's changes broke the others' assumptions because the modules had no contracts between them, only proximity. Splitting the service along the four existing team lines reduced the coordination tax; it did not eliminate cross-team dependencies — those moved into explicit, versioned contracts. (ilustratif — composite of a common failure mode; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Domain purity vs. org reality**: the technically right boundary that cuts across teams will erode back toward the team lines anyway. Either move the people or accept the seam; pretending the org does not exist does not survive a deadline.
- **Reuse vs. autonomy**: one shared service saves code but couples every team's release calendar; duplicated small code with clear owners often ships faster.
- **Conway vs. stability**: constantly reorganizing teams means constantly drifting architecture — pair each reorg with migration budget, or the system pays a tax the org never sees.

## Related principles

- [Gall's Law](/docs/principles/architecture/gall-law) — the org and the system must co-evolve; neither is designed once.
- [Single Responsibility](/docs/principles/architecture/single-responsibility) — one owner, one reason to change.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — cross-team seams need declared schemas, not proximity.
- [Versioned Contracts](/docs/principles/api/versioned-contracts) — how teams change a shared interface without breaking each other.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — ownership boundaries also limit how far a failure spreads.

## References

- Melvin Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", 1967: http://www.melconway.com/Home/Committees_Paper.html (verified URL).
- The "inverse Conway maneuver" — deliberately reshaping teams toward a target architecture — is discussed in Skelton and Pais, *Team Topologies* (verification: perlu).

---

## Single Responsibility
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/architecture/single-responsibility
- Category: architecture · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: A module should have one reason to change — scatter responsibilities and every change becomes a cross-cutting risk.
> Keep every module, service, and component to one reason to change. When you are about to add database, email, or PDF logic to a shared utility class, stop and create a focused module instead. During review, ask which single role would request this change — if several unrelated roles would, split the code before merging.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

A module has one responsibility when exactly one force — one team, one business rule, one kind of change — would ever require modifying it. Responsibility is about reasons to change, not lines of code. Once unrelated changes flow through the same file, every release couples teams, tests, and failure modes that have nothing to do with each other.

## When to use

- Designing service and module boundaries, especially shared libraries that other teams consume.
- Deciding where new code belongs — "does this fit here?" is a Single Responsibility question.
- Noticing that the same files keep changing for unrelated reasons across sprints.
- Splitting a monolith: cut along responsibility seams, not technical layers.

## When NOT to use

- One-off scripts and small tools where decomposition adds indirection but no safety.
- Early prototypes where responsibilities are still being discovered — split once they stabilize.
- Orchestration layers whose genuine single responsibility is coordinating several steps.
- Measured, performance-critical inner loops where an extra indirection has a real, proven cost.

## Anti-pattern

- A `Utils`, `Common`, or `Manager` class that accumulates every team's leftovers.
- A service function that renders a PDF, writes the database, and sends the email.
- "Just one more helper" on a shared component until every team's changes conflict.
- UI components that fetch data, transform it, and render it — three reasons to change in one file.

## Code example

Wrong — one module, three reasons to change (layout, persistence, delivery):

```ts
// utils.ts — designers, the DBA, and ops all break this file
export class Utils {
  static async invoice(order: Order) {
    const pdf = renderInvoice(order);          // designers change this
    await db.orders.insert(order.audit);       // the DBA changes this
    await smtp.send(invoiceMail(order, pdf));  // ops changes this
  }
}
```

Right — one reason to change per module, wired by the caller:

```ts
// billing/invoice-pdf.ts — changes only when the layout changes
export const renderInvoice = (o: Order) => pdf.build(layoutFor(o));
// billing/order-store.ts — changes only when persistence changes
export const saveOrder = (o: Order) => db.orders.insert(o.audit);
// notify/mailer.ts — changes only when delivery changes
export const sendInvoiceMail = (o: Order, p: Pdf) => smtp.send(invoiceMail(o, p));
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced by boundaries, not by intentions:

- **Import boundary rules in CI** (dependency-cruiser, eslint-plugin-boundaries): declare what each folder may import; shared utilities may not import infrastructure.
- **CODEOWNERS**: one owning team per module — a PR touching two owners' modules is an automatic signal to split.
- **Size and cohesion gates**: lint limits on file length and exported symbols act as smell detectors, not hard laws.
- **Review question**: "who would ask for this change?" — more than one answer means more than one responsibility.

## Real-world case

An invoicing team kept a shared `Utils` class "to avoid bikeshedding structure". Over two years it grew PDF rendering, tax rounding, database access, and an SMTP client. Every release train waited on it: marketing changed the layout, finance changed rounding, ops changed the mail relay — all in one file, all conflicting. A rounding hotfix once shipped with an unintended PDF change because both lived in the same function. Splitting earlier would not have prevented every incident, but it would have reduced each one to a single-team, single-file revert. (ilustratif — composite of a common failure mode; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Single Responsibility vs. KISS**: every split costs files and indirection. Split when the second reason to change actually arrives, not preemptively for imagined futures.
- **Single Responsibility vs. DRY Tension**: deduplication pulls similar code together; this principle pushes different reasons apart. Extract shared code only when both copies would change for the same reason.
- **Splitting vs. coherence**: cutting past the point of shared context scatters one idea across many files. A module should be as small as its responsibility — and no smaller.

## Related principles

- [Dependency Inversion](/docs/principles/architecture/dependency-inversion) — separate policy from infrastructure so responsibilities stay clean.
- [Gall's Law](/docs/principles/architecture/gall-law) — responsibilities are discovered in running code, not designed up front.
- [KISS](/docs/principles/design/kiss) — weigh every split against the indirection it adds.
- [DRY Tension](/docs/principles/design/dry-tension) — duplication across reasons beats false unification.
- [Least Astonishment](/docs/principles/design/least-astonishment) — one predictable home per behavior.

## References

- Robert C. Martin, SOLID writings — the Single Responsibility Principle as the "S" (verification: perlu — locate the specific essay before citing precisely).
- Martin, *Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices* — book-length treatment of cohesion and change (verification: perlu).

---

## Dependency Inversion
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/architecture/dependency-inversion
- Category: architecture · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: High-level policy depends on abstractions, not on concrete details — so infrastructure can change without rewriting the core.
> Make business logic depend on interfaces it owns, and push concrete SDKs, drivers, and clients to the outer layers. Never import a vendor package directly from domain code — define the port first, then adapt the vendor to it. When tests need live vendor credentials to exercise core logic, treat that as the signal to invert the dependency.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

High-level policy — billing rules, booking logic, whatever the business pays for — must not depend on low-level details such as a payment SDK, a database driver, or an HTTP client. Both sides depend on an abstraction, and crucially the abstraction belongs to the high-level side: it speaks the domain's language, not the vendor's. Details then plug into the core, so swapping or faking infrastructure stops being a rewrite.

## When to use

- Core domain logic that must be testable without network, disk, or vendor accounts.
- Infrastructure with a realistic chance of replacement: payment providers, storage backends, mail relays, message brokers.
- Library design: consumers code against your surface, not your internals.
- Multiple deployment targets — cloud versus on-prem, different regional providers.

## When NOT to use

- Wrappers built "just in case" around a single SDK with no second implementation in sight — speculative abstraction.
- Thin infrastructure code whose entire job is talking to one vendor — an adapter that only renames the vendor's API adds friction, not freedom.
- Short-lived scripts and prototypes where the rewrite cost is near zero.
- Wrapping a technology whose full power is the point, such as a search engine's query language — the abstraction will leak.

## Anti-pattern

- `BillingService` importing the payment SDK directly: policy welded to a vendor.
- An "abstraction" that is a 1:1 mirror of the vendor SDK, including its error model.
- Interfaces defined inside the vendor wrapper package — the domain now depends on the detail it was escaping.
- Test suites that require live third-party credentials because there is no seam to fake.

## Code example

Wrong — the domain imports the vendor; every provider change is core surgery:

```ts
// billing/billing-service.ts
import Stripe from 'stripe';
export class BillingService {
  async charge(cart: Cart) {
    const s = new Stripe(process.env.STRIPE_KEY!);
    const charge = await s.charges.create({ amount: cart.totalCents });
    return charge.id; // the domain now knows Stripe's response shape
  }
}
```

Right — the domain owns the port; the vendor is a replaceable detail:

```ts
// billing/payment-gateway.ts — the domain's language, the domain's file
export interface PaymentGateway { charge(cart: Cart): Promise; }
// infra/stripe-gateway.ts — the only file that knows Stripe exists
export const stripeGateway = (key: string): PaymentGateway => ({
  async charge(cart) {
    const s = new Stripe(key);
    return toReceipt(await s.charges.create({ amount: cart.totalCents }));
  },
});
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced by the build, not by intentions:

- **Import boundary rules in CI** (dependency-cruiser, eslint-plugin-boundaries): domain folders may not import infrastructure or vendor packages — the violation fails the build.
- **Architecture tests**: ts-arch or ArchUnit-style rules asserting that ports live in the domain layer and implementations outside it.
- **Test seam proof**: core logic unit tests run against an in-memory fake gateway, with no network and no vendor credentials — if they cannot, the dependency is not inverted.
- **Review checklist**: does any file under domain or core import an SDK? If yes, stop and define the port first.

## Real-world case

A subscription product hard-wired its billing core to one payment provider's SDK — charges, refunds, retries, and even error handling were written in the vendor's terms. When contract renegotiation made switching providers necessary, the "integration" turned into a multi-month rewrite: the vendor's concepts had become load-bearing inside core business rules. A domain-owned gateway port with per-provider adapters would have reduced the switch from a rewrite to an adapter project plus a careful data migration. (ilustratif — composite of a common failure mode; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Dependency Inversion vs. YAGNI**: every port and adapter is indirection someone must read. Introduce the seam when a second implementation is plausible or testing demands isolation — not for every import by default.
- **Dependency Inversion vs. KISS**: a pass-through wrapper around one SDK adds a layer with no new capability; weigh the cost of swapping later against the cost of understanding now.
- **Ports everywhere vs. Least Astonishment**: too many single-implementation interfaces turn the codebase into a maze. Keep ports few, small, and named in domain language.

## Related principles

- [Single Responsibility](/docs/principles/architecture/single-responsibility) — inversion works best when the port itself has one reason to change.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — a port is a contract: declare it and validate what crosses it.
- [Gall's Law](/docs/principles/architecture/gall-law) — extract the abstraction when the second need appears, not before.
- [YAGNI](/docs/principles/design/yagni) — the counterweight against speculative ports.
- [KISS](/docs/principles/design/kiss) — indirection is a cost; pay it only where it buys decoupling.

## References

- Robert C. Martin, SOLID writings — the Dependency Inversion Principle as the "D" (verification: perlu — locate the specific essay before citing precisely).

# Category: design

## You Aren't Gonna Need It
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/design/yagni
- Category: design · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Build for proven needs, not imagined futures — speculative generality is complexity you pay interest on forever.
> Implement only what a current, concrete requirement demands. Trace every abstraction, option, and integration to a real user story or incident; if it has none, flag it and ask a human before building. When a second real need arrives, refactor with two examples in hand rather than one guess. Treat "we might need it someday" as a cost, not a justification.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

You will be wrong about the future, so building for imagined needs means paying complexity interest on capabilities that usually never arrive — and when a real need does arrive, it rarely looks like the imagined one. YAGNI is scissors for speculative generality: the five-database config system, the plugin framework with one plugin, the flag nobody toggles. Refactoring when the second real case appears is almost always cheaper than the speculation would have been.

## When to use

- Adding any abstraction, interface, or configuration option.
- Product and architecture planning: scope is defined by what you refuse to build.
- Library design: every public export is surface you must maintain forever (see Hyrum's Law).
- Infrastructure and migration decisions with no proven consumer yet.

## When NOT to use

- Public contracts: plan additive, versioned changes for consumers you cannot coordinate with (see Versioned Contracts).
- Irreversible decisions: security fundamentals and data-layout choices that are prohibitive to retrofit are bought early, on purpose.
- Compliance, legal, and contractual requirements — even the ones with no user story.
- Capacity headroom for known, measured growth curves.

## Anti-pattern

- A storage abstraction supporting five databases when the company has run one for six years.
- A plugin system built before the second plugin exists.
- Options, strategies, and feature flags with zero production users.
- "Generalize now so we don't have to later" — later arrives with different requirements anyway.
- Dead parameter permutations that must still be tested and documented.

## Code example

Wrong — speculative generality:

```ts
// Storage layer built for five backends; we run Postgres, and only Postgres
interface ArtifactStore {
  get(id: string): Promise;
  put(id: string, blob: Buffer): Promise<void>;
  list(prefix: string): Promise<string[]>;
}
class S3Store implements ArtifactStore { /* 90 lines, never used in prod */ }
class GcsStore implements ArtifactStore { /* 90 lines, never used at all */ }
```

Right — one function for one proven need:

```ts
// Direct, boring, testable; a backend swap later is a day of work with a real spec
export async function getArtifact(id: string): Promise {
  const row = await db.query("SELECT blob FROM artifacts WHERE id = $1", [id]);
  return row.blob;
}
```

## Technical enforcement

Make speculative surface visible, then refuse it at review:

- **Dead-code and unused-export detection**: run knip / ts-prune (vulture for Python) in CI; speculative generality shows up as unreferenced exports and empty branches.
- **Option coverage rule**: any option flag with no test exercising both states fails review — if nobody tests it, nobody uses it.
- **PR template field**: "which user story or incident requires each new extension point?" — no answer, no merge.
- **Rule of three for abstractions**: the third real, independent consumer is the trigger to extract; the first is never.

## Real-world case

A platform team built a configuration system that could, on paper, target five databases, selected through a driver registry with per-driver dialect modules. The company had run a single database in production for six years. Four of the five drivers were never exercised by any real workload: they had no meaningful tests, blocked dependency upgrades, and turned every schema change into a cross-dialect negotiation. When an actual second datastore finally arrived, its query patterns did not fit the abstraction anyway, and engineers wrote a small direct client for it instead — at which point the registry supported exactly one of the two systems in use. The unused drivers were deleted years later, one upgrade-blocking release at a time. (ilustratif — composite, not a named incident; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **YAGNI vs Versioned Contracts**: internals get no speculation; public contracts are different — planning additive, versioned change for consumers you cannot coordinate with is contractual prudence, not fantasy. Speculative complexity stays banned in private code; deliberate room for change is budgeted in public contracts.
- **YAGNI vs irreversibility**: some decisions are prohibitive to retrofit — encryption at rest, data partitioning, tenant isolation. When getting it wrong later is catastrophic, buying early is risk management, not speculation (see Blast Radius).
- **YAGNI vs option pressure**: stakeholders ask for "just an option" because options look free. They are not: each one is a permutation to test, document, and maintain forever — negotiate scope down instead of options up.

## Related principles

- [Keep It Simple](/docs/principles/design/kiss) — speculative features are the main source of accidental complexity.
- [DRY, With Judgment](/docs/principles/design/dry-tension) — the rule of three before extracting shared code.
- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — whatever you ship becomes depended on, so do not ship speculative surface.
- [Gall's Law](/docs/principles/architecture/gall-law) — grow the system from what works, not from a blueprint of the future.
- [Versioned Contracts](/docs/principles/api/versioned-contracts) — where planning for change is the job.

## References

- Kent Beck, *Extreme Programming Explained* (Addison-Wesley) — YAGNI as an XP discipline: implement what you need now, defer everything else until asked for. (verification: ok — widely available).

---

## Keep It Simple
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/design/kiss
- Category: design · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Choose the simplest design that works — every moving part you add today is a part someone must debug at 3 a.m. tomorrow.
> Prefer the simplest design that satisfies the stated requirement. When two approaches both work, choose the one with fewer moving parts, fewer dependencies, and fewer concepts a reader must hold at once. Require an explicit justification for every source of complexity before implementing it. Do not add machinery for imagined future needs.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

Given two designs that both meet the requirement, the simpler one wins: fewer parts, fewer dependencies, fewer concepts to hold in your head. Complexity is not a feature — it is debt that accrues interest every time someone reads, tests, debugs, or extends the code. Simple here means the smallest number of moving parts that satisfies today's proven requirements, not the shortest or cleverest code.

## When to use

- Choosing between implementation strategies for any new component.
- Design and code review: complexity must justify itself; simplicity never has to.
- Debugging and incident response — the simplest reproduction and the simplest fix win.
- Anything read more often than written: scripts, configs, runbooks, on-call tooling.

## When NOT to use

- Failure handling for real, observed failure modes (timeouts, retries, backpressure) — that complexity is bought with evidence, not speculated.
- Security and safety layers — see Defense in Depth; each layer must earn its keep, but layers are not deleted for tidiness.
- Domains with irreducible essential complexity (tax rules, protocol edge cases, pricing) — hiding complexity is not removing it; a clever shortcut just moves it out of view.

## Anti-pattern

- A micro-framework built to avoid writing forty boring lines once.
- Config flags for behavior nobody uses.
- "Enterprise-ready" abstractions in a service with one caller and no roadmap.
- A ten-line function replaced by a dependency with forty transitive packages.
- Regex and one-liners that save minutes to write and cost hours to read.

## Code example

Wrong — a framework where one expression would do:

```ts
// "Flexible" free-shipping engine: three classes, one interpreter, zero needs
class RuleEngine {
  constructor(private rules: Rule[]) {}
  run(order: Order): boolean {
    return this.rules.some((r) => r.matches(order));
  }
}
const eligible = new RuleEngine([new OrPredicate(new ThresholdRule(50), new CustomerTierRule("gold"))]);
```

Right — the simplest thing that satisfies the requirement:

```ts
// One boolean: readable at 3 a.m., trivially testable, obviously correct
export function freeShippingEligible(order: Order): boolean {
  return order.total >= 50 || order.customer.tier === "gold";
}
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is not enforced by vibes. Wire it into CI:

- **Complexity linters**: enforce cyclomatic and cognitive complexity limits (ESLint `complexity`, SonarQube) plus per-function length caps; violations need an in-code justification or they fail.
- **Dependency budget**: new third-party packages require a PR description answering "what does this replace, and what does it cost in upgrade risk?".
- **Dead-code detection**: run knip / ts-prune so unused "flexibility" is visible on a dashboard and deletable.
- **Review checklist**: for every design the reviewer asks "what is the simplest version that passes the tests?" — the complex variant has to argue its way in, not the other way around.

## Real-world case

On 2 November 2019, Cloudflare deployed a rules update for its web application firewall containing a regular expression with nested quantifiers. On inputs that matched only partially, evaluation time exploded through catastrophic backtracking, spiking CPU on edge servers worldwide; error pages were served to visitors around the globe and a large fraction of traffic degraded. The complexity hid in a dozen-odd characters of a regex that looked unremarkable at review, and a staged rollout made the failure ramp up gradually rather than appear all at once. Engineers restored service by disabling the WAF globally. Simpler rule construction, or a complexity guard on pattern evaluation, would have reduced the blast radius — not the need for rules, just the size of the failure. Postmortem: https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-november-2-2019/ (verification: perlu for exact figures and timeline — read the postmortem before quoting numbers).

## Tension and trade-off

- **KISS vs Defense in Depth**: layered security reads as complexity, but each layer exists to fail differently. Simplify within layers; do not buy simplicity by deleting layers that each earn their keep.
- **KISS vs Graceful Degradation**: timeouts, retries, and fallbacks add code — yet they handle failure modes production provably hits. Spend the complexity budget on failure handling before features.
- **KISS vs Gall's Law**: the truly simple design is the one that can evolve. A design that is minimal on paper but cannot change is more complex in practice than a slightly larger one with clean seams.

## Related principles

- [You Aren't Gonna Need It](/docs/principles/design/yagni) — speculative features are the largest source of needless complexity.
- [DRY, With Judgment](/docs/principles/design/dry-tension) — every abstraction is complexity; unify only proven duplicates.
- [Gall's Law](/docs/principles/architecture/gall-law) — working systems grow from simple ones; simplicity enables evolution.
- [Defense in Depth](/docs/principles/security/defense-in-depth) — the counterweight: some complexity is load-bearing safety.

## References

- Kelly Johnson (Lockheed Skunk Works) is widely credited with the dictum; attribution is common but unverified — no primary source located (verification: perlu).
- Eric Raymond, *The Art of Unix Programming*, Rule of Simplicity — design for simplicity, add complexity only where you must. http://www.catb.org/~esr/writings/taoup/ (verification: perlu).

---

## DRY, With Judgment
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/design/dry-tension
- Category: design · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction — unify only knowledge that changes for the same reason.
> Before deduplicating, confirm the copies change for the same reason and will change together. Do not extract a shared abstraction from fewer than three real, independent consumers. Treat deliberate duplication between independently deploying teams as a decoupling decision, not a defect. If a unified abstraction has become a battleground, split it back along reason-for-change lines.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

DRY says every piece of knowledge should have one authoritative representation — but the unit of knowledge is the reason for change, not the text on screen. Duplication of FACTS is bad: one business rule expressed twice will eventually be edited once and ship a bug. Duplication of COINCIDENCE is fine: two blocks that look alike but change for different reasons should stay separate, because merging them couples things that must evolve apart.

## When to use

- A constant, formula, or business rule appears in multiple places that must agree: tax rates, retry limits, status meanings.
- A bug was fixed in one copy and rediscovered in another.
- Extracting shared code once at least two — better three — independent consumers exist and a named owner accepts maintenance.
- Consolidating modules inside a boundary one team owns end to end.

## When NOT to use

- Two teams duplicating a small client to stay independently deployable — the copy is the price of decoupling (see Conway's Law).
- Blocks that merely look similar but change for different reasons — that is coincidence, not fact.
- Fewer than three occurrences — extract on the third, not the first.
- Sharing that would cross an ownership boundary with no owner willing to maintain the result.

## Anti-pattern

- One "unified" helper with a flag for every consumer's difference — now more complex than all copies combined.
- A shared library with no owner, versioned by hope.
- Deduplicating by textual-similarity tools alone, with no judgment about why each copy exists.
- Keeping a wrong abstraction because deleting it means admitting the extraction was premature.

## Code example

Wrong — one helper for two APIs that only look alike:

```ts
// "Unified" request helper: every option exists for exactly one team
export function request(path: string, opts: ReqOpts) {
  if (opts.oauth) { /* payments-only: token refresh */ }
  if (opts.retryBudget) { /* search-only: backoff policy */ }
  if (opts.noRedirect) { /* payments-only: auditor requirement */ }
  return fetch(base(opts.env) + path, opts);
}
```

Right — two clients, two policies; the duplication is deliberate:

```ts
// Payments: per-call token, redirects forbidden, no client retry (idempotency upstream)
export async function payRequest(path: string, init: RequestInit) {
  const token = await paymentsToken();
  return fetch(PAY_BASE + path, { ...init, redirect: "error",
    headers: { ...init.headers, Authorization: token } });
}

// Search: stateless, cheap, safe to retry with a budget
export function search(q: string) {
  return withRetry(() => fetch(SEARCH_BASE + "?q=" + encodeURIComponent(q)), 3);
}
```

## Technical enforcement

Judgment is the tool, but tooling keeps the judgment honest:

- **Copy-paste detection as signal, not gate**: run jscpd / PMD CPD in CI and trend the numbers; humans decide whether each hit is fact or coincidence.
- **Rule of three in the PR template**: extracting shared code requires naming two existing independent consumers besides the author's, plus a named owner.
- **ADR for shared libraries**: a short decision record stating what the abstraction unifies, who owns it, and how it versions (see Explicit Contracts).
- **Coupling metrics**: track inbound dependencies on shared modules; a module consumed by teams with different release cadences needs an explicit versioning policy or a split.

## Real-world case

Two teams — payments and search — each had a small HTTP client. A well-meaning engineer unified them into one request helper with options covering both. Over the following year the two upstream APIs evolved apart: different auth models, retry semantics, error payloads. Every change to the helper broke one team; every fix added a flag; the file accumulated options nobody could fully test, and PRs on it became cross-team negotiations. Both teams started routing around it with local wrappers. The helper was finally split back into two focused clients, each smaller than the shared one, and velocity recovered — the duplication had never been the problem; the premature unification was. (ilustratif — composite of common failure modes, not a named incident; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **DRY vs decoupling**: two teams duplicating a two-hundred-line client to stay independently deployable can be right — the shared version couples their release trains forever. Where Conway's Law draws a real organizational boundary, code duplication is often the correct reflection of it.
- **DRY vs premature abstraction**: an abstraction extracted from one example encodes today's guess about tomorrow's variation; when reality diverges, every caller fights it, and the wrong abstraction costs more to unwind than the duplication it replaced. The rule of three exists to force at least two real data points before unifying anything.
- **Facts vs coincidence — the operational test**: duplication of FACTS (one rule that must change in lockstep: a rate, a status code, a formula) eventually ships the bug where one copy was missed — unify it. Duplication of COINCIDENCE (looks similar, changes for different reasons) buys independent evolution — leave it, and leave a comment saying it is deliberate.

## Related principles

- [Single Responsibility](/docs/principles/architecture/single-responsibility) — unify along exactly one reason to change.
- [Conway's Law](/docs/principles/architecture/conways-law) — org boundaries decide whether shared code is a bridge or a battleground.
- [You Aren't Gonna Need It](/docs/principles/design/yagni) — the rule of three is YAGNI applied to abstraction.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — shared code needs an explicit, versioned contract.
- [Least Astonishment](/docs/principles/design/least-astonishment) — a shared abstraction must not surprise either consumer.

## References

- Hunt & Thomas, *The Pragmatic Programmer* (Addison-Wesley) — origin of DRY; framed there as a principle about knowledge, not about text. (verification: ok — widely available; verify exact wording against your edition before quoting verbatim).

---

## Chesterton's Fence
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/design/chesterton-fence
- Category: design · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Never remove a fence until you know why it was built — in code, the comment is rarely where the reason lives.
> Before deleting or changing code you did not write, find out why it exists: git history, tests, linked incidents, and the people who were present. Treat unexplained code as load-bearing until proven otherwise. If you cannot establish why a fence was built, do not remove it — escalate to someone who may know. Land removals as small, separately revertable changes with monitoring attached.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

Chesterton's fence: a reformer sees a fence across a field and demands its removal; the owner refuses until the reformer can say why it was put there. In code the fence is the weird branch, the extra validation, the delay nobody can explain, the flag nobody remembers — and the reason is rarely in a comment; it lives in an incident, a customer escalation, or a five-year-old commit message. Changing what you do not understand is not refactoring; it is guessing with production traffic.

## When to use

- Touching legacy code with unclear invariants.
- Reviewing deletion and "cleanup" PRs.
- Infrastructure changes: security groups, cron schedules, retry loops, timeouts.
- Repurposing old names — flags, config keys, status codes, endpoints.

## When NOT to use

- When the fence is provably a leftover: verified dead code with no callers, no references in configs or docs, and a history showing why it died — delete it (see YAGNI).
- When the behavior is captured by an executable test that documents the invariant — the reason now lives in the suite, not in oral history.
- Greenfield code you wrote yourself, before anyone depends on it.

## Anti-pattern

- "This looks dead, deleting." as the entire PR description.
- Repurposing an existing flag for new behavior because the name is close enough.
- Removing a validation "because it rejects our new valid input" without finding the bad input it was rejecting.
- Big-bang cleanup PRs deleting fifty unexplained things in one diff.
- Mixing a cleanup into an unrelated feature change, so neither can be reverted alone.

## Code example

Wrong — removing the fence by looks:

```ts
// PR title: "cleanup: remove pointless delay in order submit"
async function submit(order: Order) {
  return api.submit(order); // delay removed — nobody knew what it was for
}
```

Right — find the reason first, then decide:

```ts
// The delay sheds load from a downstream queue that drops bursts
// (incident 2021-04, now documented in ADR-114).
// Keep it until the queue fix ships; remove BOTH together.
async function submit(order: Order) {
  await delay(1500);
  return api.submit(order);
}
```

## Technical enforcement

Fences are cheap to respect when process demands evidence:

- **Deletion evidence rule**: PRs that delete code must link their proof — git blame summary, no-caller evidence from static analysis (knip, vulture), or the incident that introduced the code. "Looks dead" is not evidence.
- **Quarantine before delete**: prefer disable-behind-a-flag plus a monitoring window over hard deletion, expand-contract style, so the removal itself is revertable.
- **Staged rollout with auto-rollback**: deploy deletion changes canary-first with alerting on the affected path (see Blast Radius, Observability First).
- **Review checklist**: the reviewer must be able to answer "why did this exist?" — if neither author nor reviewer can, the deletion waits.

## Real-world case

On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital deployed new code for its Retail Liquidity Program. The new code repurposed an old feature flag that had once activated a deactivated "Power Peg" order function — code that had been left on servers rather than removed. The deployment reached only seven of eight servers. When markets opened, orders carrying the repurposed flag triggered the dormant Power Peg code on the missed server — a safeguard that had once bounded it had been retired years earlier — and it pumped erroneous orders into the market for the better part of an hour. Knight lost more than USD 460 million and survived only through acquisition. A verified deployment would have reduced that day's damage; not reusing a flag whose old meaning was still live in production would have removed the failure mode. SEC order: https://www.sec.gov/litigation/admin/2013/34-70694.pdf (verification: ok for the incident and the order; perlu for exact figures — read the order before quoting precise numbers).

## Tension and trade-off

- **Fence-keeping vs code hygiene**: dead code is a real liability — bit-rot, review cost, false confidence. The rule is not "never delete"; it is "understand, then delete." Verified-dead code should go (see YAGNI).
- **Fence-hunting vs velocity**: waiting for the one engineer who knows a subsystem costs days. Mitigate with small, revertable deletions under monitoring rather than big-bang removal — or ship the removal behind a flag first.
- **Oral history vs codified knowledge**: a fence whose reason lives in one person's memory is already failing. The durable fix is moving the reason into tests, ADRs, and runbooks — making the intent observable, not just the behavior.

## Related principles

- [Observability First](/docs/principles/reliability/observability-first) — you cannot judge a fence you cannot see working.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — stage deletions so the worst case is small.
- [Expand-Contract](/docs/principles/data/expand-contract) — remove in safe phases; never big-bang.
- [Single Responsibility](/docs/principles/architecture/single-responsibility) — the Knight flag failed by carrying two meanings at once.
- [You Aren't Gonna Need It](/docs/principles/design/yagni) — the counterweight for code that is provably dead.

## References

- G.K. Chesterton, *The Thing* (1929) — the fence parable; commonly located in the essay "The Drift from Domesticity" (verification: ok for the book and year; locate the exact passage before quoting verbatim).
- SEC Administrative Order, Release No. 34-70694 (2013) — In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC. https://www.sec.gov/litigation/admin/2013/34-70694.pdf
