## Principle of Least Astonishment
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/design/least-astonishment
- Category: design · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Do what the reader expects — match conventions so the obvious reading is the correct one.
> Make the obvious reading the correct one: names, defaults, and API shapes must follow the dominant convention of the platform. State every side effect of an operation in its name, documentation, or response. Before shipping a behavior, ask whether a reader could predict it from the signature alone. If it would surprise you as a caller, change it or document it loudly.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

A component is well designed when its behavior matches what a competent reader predicts from its name, signature, and surrounding conventions. Surprise is a design bug even when the behavior is technically correct — the reader acts on their wrong assumption, and the damage lands in data. Conventions do most of the work: following the platform's defaults is usually more important than being locally clever.

## When to use

- Naming anything public: endpoints, functions, flags, config keys.
- Choosing defaults — the default should be the safest and most common case, not the most flexible one.
- API and library surface design, including error and empty responses.
- UX flows and CLI interactions where muscle memory carries users.

## When NOT to use

- When the convention itself is dangerous — surprising-but-safe beats familiar-and-destructive (see Secure by Default).
- Legacy surfaces with many existing callers — changing surprising-but-shipped behavior breaks the world (see Hyrum's Law); version the change instead.
- Domains with no established convention — your choice becomes the convention; make it once, centrally, and document it prominently.

## Anti-pattern

- A delete endpoint that also deletes dependent records without saying so.
- A getter that writes; a list method that paginates differently from every other list in the codebase.
- Flags whose names promise less than they do — a purgeCache that also drops connections.
- Errors swallowed and replaced with empty success responses.
- Timezone-naive or locale-naive defaults in a global product.

## Code example

Wrong — "helpful" magic:

```ts
// DELETE /users/:id — also silently wipes the user's invoices and tokens
async function deleteUser(id: string) {
  await db.users.delete(id);
  await db.invoices.deleteMany({ userId: id }); // surprise: undocumented cascade
  await db.tokens.deleteMany({ userId: id });   // surprise: sessions die silently
}
```

Right — the obvious reading is the correct reading:

```ts
// Deleting a user deletes a user. Nothing else.
async function deleteUser(id: string) {
  await db.users.delete(id);
}

// Purging data is a separate, named, explicit operation
async function purgeUserData(id: string) {
  await db.users.delete(id);
  const invoices = await db.invoices.deleteMany({ userId: id });
  return { deletedInvoices: invoices.count }; // the response admits what happened
}
```

## Technical enforcement

Surprise is testable if you make it so:

- **Contract tests**: automated tests assert that each endpoint performs only its documented effects; an undocumented cascade fails CI.
- **API review checklist**: "list every effect this operation has — is each one in the name, the docs, or the response?" No unlisted effects ship.
- **Schema enforcement**: OpenAPI (or equivalent) schemas are validated against actual responses in CI, so surprises surface before consumers do.
- **Convention linting**: naming rules for flags, config keys, and endpoints; divergence from the project's established patterns requires an ADR.

## Real-world case

An internal platform exposed a delete endpoint for user records. To "save callers a round trip," it also deleted the user's dependent records — invoices, API keys, audit entries — without documenting or reporting the cascade. Callers, patterned on every other delete endpoint in the company (which returned a conflict when dependencies existed), assumed a single-row delete. A routine offboarding script removed hundreds of dependent records in one afternoon; because the cascade was silent, the loss was found days later by reconciliation, not by the operator. The fix was not just documentation: the cascade became a separate, explicit purge endpoint whose response reports everything it removed — reducing, not preventing, the damage of the next wrong assumption. (ilustratif — composite, not a named incident; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Least Astonishment vs Postel's Robustness**: silently accepting and repairing malformed input is also a surprise — the caller never learns their request was wrong. Prefer explicit contracts with loud, actionable errors over quiet forgiveness.
- **Least Astonishment vs Hyrum's Law**: whatever you ship becomes load-bearing; surprising behavior that has already shipped cannot simply be fixed without breaking its dependents. Version the correction (see Versioned Contracts).
- **Convenience vs predictability**: convention-over-configuration and smart defaults save insiders time and astonish newcomers. Budget the magic, and make the hidden defaults discoverable.

## Related principles

- [Postel's Robustness](/docs/principles/api/postel-robustness) — the perennial counterweight: leniency in what you accept.
- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — shipped behavior, wanted or not, becomes the contract.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — effects documented and enforced are effects that cannot surprise.
- [Soft Delete](/docs/principles/data/soft-delete) — reversible deletion reduces the cost of a wrong assumption.
- [Fail Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — when surprise happens anyway, it must be seen.

## References

- Eric Raymond, *The Art of Unix Programming*, Rule of Least Surprise — design interfaces that match the culture's expectations. http://www.catb.org/~esr/writings/taoup/ (verification: perlu).

---

## Goodhart's Law
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/design/goodharts-law
- Category: design · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — proxy metrics get gamed by exactly the optimizers you point at them.
> Never set or optimize a single proxy metric without pairing it with a counter-metric that exposes gaming. Before committing to a target, ask how a motivated optimizer would raise the number without improving the underlying goal, then instrument for exactly that. Treat any metric tied to evaluation or compensation as already under pressure. Report balanced panels, never lone numbers.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

A metric is a proxy for something you actually care about — coverage proxies for safety, uptime proxies for user experience, velocity proxies for value. The moment the proxy becomes the target, effort flows into moving the number rather than the thing it stood for, because moving the number is easier. The optimizers doing this are usually not cheating; they are doing precisely what you pointed them at.

## When to use

- Setting team goals, SLAs, and performance incentives.
- ML work: choosing and freezing an objective function — reward hacking is Goodhart's Law with gradient descent.
- Choosing test-coverage, uptime, latency, or velocity targets.
- Building dashboards that other people will act on.

## When NOT to use

- As an argument against measurement altogether — unmeasured systems fail silently (see Observability First); the fix is paired metrics, not blindness.
- During exploration: leading indicators that guide discovery are fine as long as nobody's evaluation depends on them.
- One-off diagnostic readings that are never promoted into targets.

## Anti-pattern

- A 100% line-coverage mandate — the cheapest path is tests that execute code and assert nothing.
- Bonuses tied to a single number: uptime, tickets closed, lines removed.
- Model evaluation on a benchmark that has effectively become the training set.
- Ranking teams on a dashboard they can see — visibility accelerates gaming.
- Renaming a gamed metric and continuing as before.

## Code example

Wrong — the metric satisfied, the goal abandoned:

```ts
// Written to close the coverage ticket: line runs, nothing is checked
it("processes refunds", () => {
  processRefund(paidOrder); // exception-free execution counts as "covered"
  expect(true).toBe(true);  // the assertion is decorative
});
```

Right — pair the target with a counter-metric:

```ts
// Mutation testing rewards assertions that can actually fail
it("refunds the card and marks the order refunded", async () => {
  const result = await processRefund(paidOrder);
  expect(result.status).toBe("refunded");
  expect(gateway.refunds).toHaveLength(1); // money actually moved
  const stored = await orders.find(paidOrder.id);
  expect(stored.state).toBe("refunded");   // state actually persisted
});
```

## Technical enforcement

Gaming is a systems property; fight it with system design:

- **Metric pairing policy**: every target ships with a counter-metric in the same view — coverage with mutation score, velocity with escaped-defect rate, uptime with change-failure rate and recovery time.
- **Mutation testing in CI** (Stryker, PIT, mutmut) as the counter-metric for coverage: assertions that cannot fail let mutants survive, and surviving mutants fail the build.
- **No single-metric compensation**: tie evaluation to balanced panels (DORA-style sets), never to one number.
- **Target review cadence**: re-read every target quarterly and ask "how is this being gamed right now?"; rotate or retire gamed metrics rather than defending them.

## Real-world case

An engineering group set a 100% line-coverage target for a critical service, with review scores tied to it. Coverage climbed within a quarter — and a growing share of new tests were hollow: they invoked code with fixture data and asserted nothing stronger than "did not throw," or snapshotted empty mocks. The number said safe; escaped defects said otherwise, and incidents kept tracing to branches the metric counted as covered. The target was replaced with a paired panel: coverage thresholds plus mutation score, with assert-less tests flagged automatically. The hollow tests started failing CI, and while the coverage number went down, real defect detection went up. (ilustratif — composite of widely reported failure modes, not a named incident; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Goodhart vs Observability First**: measurement is not the enemy — unmeasured systems drift silently. The rule is pairing, not abstinence: every metric gets a counter-metric tuned to catch its specific gaming strategy.
- **Goodhart vs simplicity of process**: a single north-star number is easy to communicate and easy to game; a small balanced panel is harder to communicate and harder to game. Pay the communication cost.
- **Goodhart vs ML optimization**: models are literal Goodhart engines — they will exploit any gap between reward and intent (reward hacking). Hold out ground-truth evaluation the optimizer never sees, and keep humans in the loop on objective changes.

## Related principles

- [Observability First](/docs/principles/reliability/observability-first) — you need the metrics; just never one alone.
- [Fail Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — gamed proxies hide failures; make the real failures loud.
- [Keep It Simple](/docs/principles/design/kiss) — minimal dashboards are simpler; simplicity of the metric and honesty of the signal trade off.
- [Chesterton's Fence](/docs/principles/design/chesterton-fence) — before removing or renaming a long-standing metric, find out why it was installed.

## References

- Marilyn Strathern, 1997 formulation — "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" (verification: perlu — locate the precise paper and page before quoting; commonly attributed to her 1997 work on British university audit).
- Google SRE Book — monitoring and alerting practice; alerting on symptoms rather than causes is a partial structural mitigation. https://sre.google/sre-book/

---

# Category: reliability

## Fail Visible
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible
- Category: reliability · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Fail loudly and immediately — silent failure converts a small bug into corrupted state discovered weeks later.
> Make every failure loud, immediate, and attributable: raise the error, exit nonzero, fail the build. Never swallow exceptions, never return a default value after a failed operation, never continue past a failed precondition. A silent partial result is worse than a crash — if you cannot classify a failure as harmless, surface it to a human.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Fail-visible means errors announce themselves at the point of failure — an exception, a nonzero exit, a red build — instead of propagating wrong data downstream. The alternative, silent failure, converts a five-minute fix into weeks of corrupted state: the system keeps "working" while quietly lying. Fail-fast is the operational half of the rule: the sooner a defect stops execution, the closer the stop is to the defect that caused it.

## When to use

- Data pipelines: a bad record must divert loudly, not zero out a field and continue.
- CI/CD and scripts: nonzero exits and red builds; a check that turns green while doing nothing is lying.
- Library design: invalid input or impossible state raises, never guesses intent.
- Distributed calls: timeouts and errors returned to the caller, never absorbed into defaults.

## When NOT to use

- Best-effort UI niceties (a failed avatar shows a placeholder) — that is graceful degradation, and the difference is intent: a designed, visible fallback, not an accidental swallow.
- Transient errors inside a supervised retry loop — provided the supervisor alarms once the budget is spent (see Retry Budget).
- Security-critical verification paths, where "fail" must additionally mean "fail closed" — visible but open is a breach (see Fail-Safe Defaults).

## Anti-pattern

- An except clause that swallows everything and returns None — callers cannot distinguish "no data" from "could not check".
- A CI check that exits zero when its own tooling is missing, "so the build stays green".
- Errors written to a log nobody reads while the API returns success.
- Falling back to default config when config parsing fails — the service runs with unknown settings.
- A verification function that returns success when an internal step did not run.

## Code example

Wrong — validation silently bypassed:

```python
def find_user_or_none(payload):
    try:
        return store.find_user(payload["user_id"])
    except Exception:
        return None            # caller sees "no such user"; the store being down is invisible
```

Right — loud, immediate, attributable:

```python
def find_user(payload):
    try:
        return store.find_user(payload["user_id"])
    except KeyError as e:
        raise InvalidPayload(f"missing field {e}")          # input error, named
    except StoreUnavailable as e:
        raise LookupFailed("user store unreachable") from e  # infra error, chained, visible
```

## Technical enforcement

Silence is a lint and design problem — enforce it mechanically:

- **Lint rules**: empty catch blocks and blanket exception swallowing fail CI in most linters' default rule sets; enable them.
- **Script discipline**: the project's bash template ships with strict error mode (exit on error, fail on unset variables, fail on pipe failure); every script inherits it.
- **Dead-man switches**: processes that must keep running publish heartbeats; absence of the heartbeat is the alarm — a silent zombie cannot hide.
- **Review checklist**: every new except/catch branch must name what it does with the error.
- **Aggregate visibility**: the sum of individual loud failures stays visible as an error ratio on a dashboard (see Observability First).

## Real-world case

In February 2014, Apple fixed a TLS verification bug that had been shipping in its SSL/TLS code for some time: a duplicated "goto fail;" line, executed unconditionally because the surrounding if statements used no braces, jumped to the error-handling label with a zero (success) error value. The remaining signature checks were skipped, and affected systems could accept connections regardless of the server's signature. Nothing errored, nothing logged — the failure mode was "success", and the bug could only be found by reading the code, not by watching production. Writeup: https://www.imperialviolet.org/2014/02/22/applebug.html — a single visible failure at that branch would have reduced a silent security bypass to an ordinary bug report.

## Tension and trade-off

- **Fail-Visible vs. resilience**: swallowing-and-continuing keeps demos alive but poisons data; weigh by whether wrong data is recoverable later — it usually is not.
- **Fail-Visible vs. Graceful Degradation**: fail loudly at the layer that owns the decision, degrade visibly at the layer that owns the user experience; the same error is a crash in a library and a friendly banner in the UI.
- **Weigh against Least Astonishment**: loud means clear and attributable, not noisy — a wall of identical stack traces hides the one real signal as effectively as silence does.

## Related principles

- [Observability First](/docs/principles/reliability/observability-first) — the raised error needs a metric and a trace waiting for it.
- [Graceful Degradation](/docs/principles/reliability/graceful-degradation) — deliberate, visible fallbacks at the UX layer.
- [Fail-Safe Defaults](/docs/principles/security/fail-safe-defaults) — in verification paths, failing visibly must also mean failing closed.
- [Retry Budget](/docs/principles/reliability/retry-budget) — only transient, visible errors belong in a retry loop.

## References

- Adam Langley, *Apple's SSL/TLS bug*, 2014 — https://www.imperialviolet.org/2014/02/22/applebug.html
- Waldo et al., *A Note on Distributed Computing*, 1994 — partial failure in distributed systems is silent by nature; visibility must be built (verification: perlu).
- Google SRE Book — https://sre.google/sre-book/ (postmortem culture: visible failures get fixed).

---

## Blast Radius
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius
- Category: reliability · Severity: critical · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Limit the maximum damage any single action can cause — batch size caps, per-step confirmations, and staged rollouts turn catastrophes into incidents.
> Before executing any state-changing or infrastructure command, ask what is the worst this single action can do — then cap that worst case. Break destructive work into small batches with a dry-run and a fresh confirmation per step, and prefer staged rollouts over fleet-wide changes. If you cannot state the exact set of resources a command will touch, stop and ask a human.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: critical.**

## Definition

The blast radius of an action is the amount of state, traffic, or infrastructure it can damage in one execution. Engineer the maximum, not the average: the probability of a typo is fixed, but whether a typo kills one shard or the whole fleet is a design choice. Batch caps, per-step confirmation, and staged rollout are how the worst case gets a ceiling.

## When to use

- Commands that delete, drop, restart, or remove in bulk — filesystem, database, cloud.
- Deployments and infrastructure changes: canaries, percentages, one environment at a time.
- Data migrations and backfills over live production tables.
- ML: bulk dataset deletes, model promotion, cluster-wide retraining jobs.
- Recovery tooling: keep it outside the failure domain of the thing it recovers.

## When NOT to use

- Genuinely small atomic operations — a single-row insert does not need chunking.
- Explicitly disposable sandboxes where the worst case is "recreate it in ten minutes".
- Emergency kill switches that must act globally and immediately — their speed is the point; scope the trust instead (see Least Authority).

## Anti-pattern

- "DELETE FROM users" with the WHERE clause added mentally rather than literally.
- A debugging command typed at 3am whose scope is "everything that matches".
- One deploy pipeline applying one plan to every environment at once.
- Recovery and monitoring tools that live inside the blast radius they are meant to survive.

## Code example

Wrong — one command, unbounded scope:

```bash
# "Clean up the old backups" — no cap, no dry-run, no confirmation
find /var/backups -type f -name '*.gz' | xargs rm -f
```

Right — bounded batch, printed plan, fresh confirmation:

```bash
./bin/purge --older-than 30d --limit 500 --dry-run   # step 1: print the exact target set
./bin/purge --older-than 30d --limit 500 --confirm   # step 2: delete only what was printed
./bin/purge --older-than 30d --limit 500 --confirm   # step 3: next batch, verify between
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced by tooling and permissions, not by operator discipline:

- **IAM scoping**: no standing role can destroy resources across environments; destructive verbs are per-environment and require fresh escalation.
- **Tooling defaults**: dry-run is the default mode; a row/resource limit is required on destructive verbs; multi-batch runs re-confirm with a human between batches.
- **Migration guards**: the migration tool refuses a DELETE or UPDATE touching more than N rows without a special, reviewed flag.
- **Staged rollout as config**: percentage-based deployment with automatic halt on error-rate or latency regression is the only approved deploy path.
- **Out-of-band recovery**: consoles, DNS, and monitoring run on separate credentials and networks from the systems they protect.

## Real-world case

On 2017-02-28, while debugging a slow S3 billing subsystem, an authorized S3 team member ran a command meant to remove a small number of servers for that one subsystem. One input was entered incorrectly, and the command removed a larger set of servers than intended — additional S3 subsystems went down with it and required a full restart. The blast radius of a single mistyped command, executed inside shared infrastructure, became hours of unavailability for the many sites and services that depend on S3 in that region. Postmortem: https://aws.amazon.com/message/41926/ — a smaller, confirmed scope would have reduced a regional outage to a maintenance task.

On 2021-10-04, Facebook ran a maintenance command intended to assess the availability of its global backbone; it instead unplugged the connections between the backbone and the data centers, Facebook's routes were withdrawn from the internet, and the platform became unreachable worldwide. Crucially for this principle, DNS, internal tools, and out-of-band management were reachable only through the same affected network — the recovery tools were inside the blast radius. Engineers needed physical access to the machines to restore service. Postmortem: https://engineering.fb.com/2021/10/04/networking-traffic/october-4-2021-outage/ — out-of-band tooling would have reduced the outage from a physical trip to a remote fix.

## Tension and trade-off

- **Speed vs. containment**: capped batches and staged rollouts trade minutes for the guarantee that a mistake is small. Weigh by the value of what is touched, not by operator patience.
- **Cost vs. isolation**: keeping recovery and monitoring out-of-band costs money every day it is unused — and repays itself the one time it is needed.
- **Weigh against Least Authority**: scoping who may act and scoping what any action may damage are complementary; neither substitutes for the other.

## Related principles

- [Least Authority](/docs/principles/security/least-authority) — who can act; blast radius is what any action can hit.
- [Idempotency](/docs/principles/reliability/idempotency) — a repeated action stays as small as the first one.
- [Tested Backups](/docs/principles/data/tested-backups) — the last line of defense when containment was not enough.
- [Graceful Degradation](/docs/principles/reliability/graceful-degradation) — contain damage at runtime, not just at deploy time.

## References

- AWS, *Summary of the Amazon S3 Service Disruption*, 2017 — https://aws.amazon.com/message/41926/
- Facebook Engineering, *October 4, 2021 Outage* — https://engineering.fb.com/2021/10/04/networking-traffic/october-4-2021-outage/
- Google SRE Book — https://sre.google/sre-book/ (change management and release engineering practice).

---

## Retry Budget
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/reliability/retry-budget
- Category: reliability · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Retries amplify outages — use exponential backoff with jitter and a hard budget on total retry volume.
> Treat every retry as a bet that pays off only when the failure is transient and the callee has spare capacity. Use exponential backoff with full jitter, cap attempts per request, and enforce a global budget on total retry volume — when the budget is spent, fail fast and surface the error. Never ship a retry loop that lacks all three limits.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

A retry budget is a hard, measured limit on how much extra load retries may add — for example, retries may be at most a fixed small share of all requests — combined with exponential backoff and jitter so attempts spread over time. Retries are hope converted into load; when the callee is already failing, that load lands on the weakest component and converts a blip into an outage. The budget is what keeps hope affordable.

## When to use

- Any client of a remote dependency (HTTP, RPC, database, broker) with timeout-capable calls.
- Event-driven consumers that requeue or re-deliver failed messages.
- Batch pipelines that re-run failed items.
- SDKs and libraries others will embed — their retry defaults become someone else's architecture (see Hyrum's Law).

## When NOT to use

- Non-idempotent operations without a key — retrying a payment without idempotency is a correctness bug, not resilience.
- Latency-sensitive requests whose caller already left — retrying after the user abandoned the page is pure load with no beneficiary.
- Client errors and business rejections — retrying a validation error is a loop with extra steps.
- Strictly ordered work where a delayed retry would apply state out of order.

## Anti-pattern

- Immediate retries, fixed count, no jitter — every client hammers in lockstep, exactly when the target is worst off.
- Nested retries at every layer: client, gateway, service, and database each retry three times; the multipliers compound.
- Retrying harder precisely when the dependency is overloaded — amplifying the very signal that should trigger shedding.
- Retry policy decided per call site by each developer independently, with no global view.

## Code example

Wrong — synchronized, unbounded retry:

```python
for attempt in range(3):
    try:
        return search_client.query(q)      # instant retries, in lockstep everywhere
    except Timeout:
        continue                           # no jitter, no budget, no deadline
raise SearchUnavailable(q)                 # after hammering an already-dying service
```

Right — backoff, jitter, deadline, and a global cap:

```python
def search(q, deadline):
    for attempt in range(3):
        if monotonic() >= deadline:
            raise SearchUnavailable(q)                       # caller left: stop retrying
        sleep(random.uniform(0, 0.1 * 2 ** attempt))         # exponential + full jitter
        try:
            return search_client.query(q, timeout=0.2)       # hard timeout per attempt
        except (Timeout, Unavailable):
            continue
    raise SearchUnavailable(q)
```

## Technical enforcement

Retries are a system property, not a per-developer preference — enforce them centrally:

- **Client library defaults**: backoff, jitter, attempt cap, and retry-on status list ship in the standard client; bare retry helpers are rejected in code review.
- **Retry budgets at the caller**: a token-bucket or circuit-breaker allows at most 1 retry per N requests; when the budget is empty, requests fail fast with a loud error.
- **Server-side protection**: the callee distinguishes and rejects excess retry traffic (busy responses with retry-after guidance) so callers learn instead of hammering.
- **Deadline propagation**: every request carries its remaining patience; nested retries cannot multiply beyond the caller's deadline.
- **Tests**: killing a dependency in staging must produce bounded, measurable extra load — visible as a bump, not a storm.

## Real-world case

(ilustratif) A downstream dependency blips for sixty seconds during a deploy. Every client retries immediately — three attempts, no jitter — and retry traffic exceeds normal traffic right as the dependency comes back up. The recovering service spends the next forty minutes processing a synchronized queue of retries instead of user requests; the monitoring graph shows the caller failing long after the dependency was healthy. Backoff with jitter plus a hard budget would have reduced a self-inflicted partial outage to a brief bump in error rate. (verification: perlu — retry-storm incidents are described in public postmortems; belum digali — verify specific sources before citing any of them.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Retry Budget vs. latency SLOs**: aggressive retries buy milliseconds of availability in good times and cost minutes of outage in bad times; budget for the bad times.
- **Retry Budget vs. Idempotency**: retrying is only safe where idempotency already holds; make the operation safe before making the retry automatic.
- **Weigh against Fail-Visible**: budget-exhausted failures must surface as loud errors — a framework that silently drops them converts unavailability into data loss.

## Related principles

- [Idempotency](/docs/principles/reliability/idempotency) — the precondition for any automatic retry.
- [Graceful Degradation](/docs/principles/reliability/graceful-degradation) — shed load to a failing dependency instead of feeding it.
- [Fail-Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — a spent budget must alarm, not vanish.
- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — your retry defaults become someone's production behavior.

## References

- Google SRE Book — https://sre.google/sre-book/ (handling overload and shedding excess requests).
- Google SRE Workbook — https://sre.google/workbook/ (the "Cascading Failures" chapter on retry amplification).

---

## Graceful Degradation
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/reliability/graceful-degradation
- Category: reliability · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: When a component degrades, shed the optional and keep the essential — partial service beats total outage.
> Classify every dependency as essential or optional before an outage classifies it for you. Give each outbound call a timeout, wrap it in a circuit breaker, and design a concrete fallback for every optional feature. Under overload, shed optional work first — never let a slow dependency occupy your worker threads.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

A system degrades gracefully when the failure or overload of a component reduces capability instead of availability: checkout still works while the recommendation carousel disappears. This requires classifying dependencies as essential or optional before the incident, and writing down the fallback for each optional one. Partial failure is the steady state of distributed systems; the real choice is between planned partial service and unplanned total outage.

## When to use

- User-facing pages and APIs assembled from many services: return the essential response, drop the slow enrichment.
- High-fanout request paths where one slow dependency can starve the whole worker pool.
- Traffic spikes and dependency brownouts: shed load explicitly before the process dies.
- ML systems: serve the last good model when fresh training or feature pipelines lag.

## When NOT to use

- Correctness and safety paths — auth, payments, security checks — where "degraded" means fail-open; that is fail-unsafe, not graceful (see Fail-Safe Defaults).
- Products whose essential path IS the optional component (a translation service without translation is an outage, not a degradation).
- Write paths where degraded means silently persisting incomplete data — that trades an outage for corruption (see Fail-Visible).

## Anti-pattern

- Page render blocks on a recommendations widget; one slow recs service turns every page into an error.
- Outbound calls with no timeout; a slow dependency gradually owns every worker thread.
- All-or-nothing aggregation: either every section of the response assembles or nothing is returned.
- Retrying harder into the failing dependency instead of shedding it (see Retry Budget).
- Serving degraded content with no signal at all to users or dashboards — nobody can tell healthy from degraded.

## Code example

Wrong — one optional widget holds the whole page:

```python
def render_page(user):
    recs = recs_client.get(user.id)      # no timeout, no fallback, essential path blocked
    cart = cart_client.get(user.id)
    return template(recs=recs, cart=cart)
```

Right — shed the optional, keep the essential:

```python
def render_page(user):
    cart = cart_client.get(user.id, timeout=0.1)          # essential: hard timeout
    try:
        recs = recs_client.get(user.id, timeout=0.05)     # optional: short budget
    except (Timeout, Unavailable):
        recs = Recommendations.empty()                   # fallback, not a 500
    return template(recs=recs, cart=cart)
```

## Technical enforcement

Degradation is a designed behavior, so it can be enforced as one:

- **Timeouts on every outbound call**, sized to the dependency's latency SLO — enforced by HTTP client and service mesh defaults, not per-developer discipline.
- **Circuit breakers with named fallbacks** wired at the framework level; a dependency without a fallback cannot be declared optional.
- **Admission control before resource exhaustion**: queue limits and explicit busy responses with retry guidance; the kernel OOM killer is not a load-shedding strategy.
- **Degradation must be observable**: a "served degraded" metric and a user-visible signal (empty state, stale marker) are part of the feature, not an optional extra.
- **Game days**: kill a dependency in staging on a schedule; the core path surviving is a pass criterion.

## Real-world case

On 2019-11-02, Cloudflare deployed a new WAF rule containing a regular expression that catastrophically backtracked on certain inputs. Due to a bug in the software that deploys rules, it went live on edge machines worldwide at once instead of gradually; the regex exhausted CPU on those machines, and requests worldwide returned 502s until engineers used a global kill switch to disable the WAF entirely. Postmortem: https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-november-2-2019/ — the inline security layer took the essential path down with it; requests were dropped rather than served degraded. The same postmortem is also a lesson in Blast Radius and staged rollout: the intended gradual deployment would have contained the rule's effect to a testable subset.

## Tension and trade-off

- **Graceful Degradation vs. Fail-Visible**: shedding can mask real errors; every degradation must be visible in metrics and in the response, or you trade an outage for slow, silent rot.
- **Graceful Degradation vs. Fail-Safe Defaults**: never degrade a security or safety check to preserve response time — degraded security is a breach, not an outage.
- **Weigh against Least Astonishment**: tell users what is missing or stale; a page that quietly lies about freshness erodes more trust than an honest degraded state.

## Related principles

- [Retry Budget](/docs/principles/reliability/retry-budget) — stop feeding a failing dependency; shed it instead.
- [Observability First](/docs/principles/reliability/observability-first) — degradation you cannot see is indistinguishable from failure.
- [Fail-Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — fail loudly at the layer that owns the decision, degrade at the layer that owns the user.
- [Fail-Safe Defaults](/docs/principles/security/fail-safe-defaults) — deny by default; essential checks never "degrade" to allow.

## References

- Google SRE Workbook — https://sre.google/workbook/ (the "Cascading Failures" chapter covers load shedding and resource exhaustion directly).
- Cloudflare, *Details of the Cloudflare Outage on November 2, 2019* — https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-november-2-2019/

---

## Observability First
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/reliability/observability-first
- Category: reliability · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: You cannot operate what you cannot see — logs, metrics, and traces exist before the incident, not after it.
> Never deploy or operate a system you cannot answer basic questions about — is it working, for whom, how fast, and why not — using telemetry that already exists. Instrument failure modes before shipping, and wire dashboards and alerts before the first production deploy. If the observability you needed during an incident was missing, note the gap and close it before the next one — and never let the tools you recover with depend on the system being recovered.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Observability is the ability to ask new questions about a system's internal state from its outputs, without shipping new code. The outputs — structured logs, metrics, traces — must exist before the incident, because the incident is exactly when there is no time to add them. The test: page yourself at 3am and ask whether you can localize the failing component from a dashboard in minutes, or whether you start guessing.

## When to use

- Every service before its first production deploy — "before" is the whole point.
- Migrations and schema changes: old and new paths must be comparable side by side (see Expand-Contract).
- Databases and queues: replication lag, queue depth, age of the oldest message, backup freshness.
- ML: training/serving skew, feature quality metrics, per-model error signals.

## When NOT to use

- Do not log secrets or PII — telemetry is a data breach surface (see Secrets Hygiene); redact at the emitter, not downstream.
- Do not instrument to absurd resolution where collection cost distorts the system — sample traces instead of tracing everything.
- Do not build bespoke dashboards for hypothetical questions — instrument real failure modes and the golden signals first (weigh against YAGNI).

## Anti-pattern

- "It's slow, add a log line" — in production, after the incident started.
- A single success/failure counter with no dimensions: no endpoint, tenant, region, or version to slice by.
- Unstructured prose log lines that cannot be filtered, counted, or joined.
- Alerts with no runbook, paging for everything so that no one reads anything.
- Internal tooling hosted inside the infrastructure it is supposed to observe.

## Code example

Wrong — invisible failure:

```python
try:
    charge(order)
except PaymentError:
    pass                       # or print("error") — no metric, no context, no trace
```

Right — visible failure, still loud:

```python
try:
    charge(order)
except PaymentError as e:
    log.error("charge_failed", order_id=order.id, code=e.code)   # structured, searchable
    metrics.increment("payments.failed", tags={"code": e.code})   # counted, sliceable
    trace.set_error(e)                                           # correlated request-wide
    raise                                                        # observable AND failing
```

## Technical enforcement

Observability is enforced by pipeline and process, not by good intentions:

- **Scaffold-time defaults**: every new service starts with golden-signal dashboards (error ratio, latency percentiles, saturation) and error alerts from the project template.
- **CI checks**: a route or handler that emits no standard error metric and structured error log does not pass review — "no unobserved endpoint".
- **Structured logging with a schema**: a shared library and lint rules reject ad-hoc print-style logging in production code.
- **Trace propagation middleware**: trace IDs are mandatory across service boundaries, so one slow request can be followed end to end.
- **Out-of-band hosting**: status pages, incident tooling, and monitoring run on separate infrastructure and credentials from everything they watch.
- **Runbook requirement**: an alert without a runbook link is deleted before it is allowed to page anyone.

## Real-world case

On 2021-10-04, Facebook's route withdrawal made the platform unreachable worldwide — and the same failure domain contained the tools engineers use to observe and operate the network. Internal systems, DNS, and out-of-band management were themselves unreachable; diagnosis and remote recovery were blocked, and restoration required engineers physically present at the data centers. Postmortem: https://engineering.fb.com/2021/10/04/networking-traffic/october-4-2021-outage/ — when you cannot observe, you cannot even recover. The general lesson predates and outlives this incident: recovery paths must survive the failures they exist to fix. (verification: perlu for link details — read the postmortem before quoting specifics.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Observability vs. cost**: full-resolution telemetry is expensive; sample traces and aggregate logs, but never sample away the signal that carries alerts.
- **Observability vs. privacy**: telemetry is a data breach surface — PII and secrets are redacted at the emitter, not downstream.
- **Weigh against YAGNI**: instrument the failure modes and golden signals you actually have; resist inventing metrics for hypothetical questions.

## Related principles

- [Fail-Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — the error must be raised before it can be observed.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — keep the observation tools outside the blast radius they must survive.
- [Graceful Degradation](/docs/principles/reliability/graceful-degradation) — degradation must be a visible state, not an invisible one.
- [Secrets Hygiene](/docs/principles/security/secrets-hygiene) — telemetry must never become the leak.

## References

- Google SRE Book — https://sre.google/sre-book/ (monitoring distributed systems; the four golden signals; postmortem culture).
- Facebook Engineering, *October 4, 2021 Outage* — https://engineering.fb.com/2021/10/04/networking-traffic/october-4-2021-outage/

---

## Idempotency
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/reliability/idempotency
- Category: reliability · Severity: critical · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Running the same operation twice must produce the same result as once — accidental re-runs become boring instead of fatal.
> Make every mutating operation safe to execute more than once. Attach a stable idempotency key to each write that moves money, sends side effects, or changes state, and check it before executing. If an operation cannot be made idempotent, stop and ask a human before wiring it into a retry path, a queue consumer, or a script that may run twice.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: critical.**

## Definition

An operation is idempotent when executing it N times leaves the system in the same state as executing it once. In distributed systems this is not a nicety: timeouts are ambiguous (the request may have committed), delivery guarantees are at-least-once, and humans re-run scripts. Idempotency converts "did my request land?" from a data-integrity crisis into a boring re-send.

## When to use

- Anything a client may retry: payments, order creation, provisioning, message sending.
- Queue consumers — at-least-once delivery is the honest default of most brokers.
- Cron jobs, backfills, and cleanup scripts that humans re-run after partial failures.
- ML pipelines: feature backfills, restartable training steps, dataset materialization.

## When NOT to use

- Pure reads — already safe; dedupe machinery around them is unearned complexity.
- Genuinely single-use state (a voucher being consumed) — model it as an explicit state transition, not a "safe retry".
- Cheap, re-derivable writes (cache refresh) where a duplicate is harmless by construction.

## Anti-pattern

- A charge call with no idempotency key, wrapped in a retry loop.
- A crash between the payment call and the "mark processed" update — re-delivery re-charges.
- A backfill script that starts with DELETE and trusts the operator to run it exactly once.
- Treating a timeout as "definitely failed" and repeating a non-idempotent call.

## Code example

Wrong — the retry itself is the bug:

```python
def handle_event(event):
    # No idempotency key: a timeout plus one client retry charges twice
    charge = gateway.charge(event.amount, event.token)
    db.run("UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = ?", event.order_id)
```

Right — the event's identity is the key:

```python
def handle_event(event):
    key = f"order:{event.order_id}:charge"
    if db.one("SELECT 1 FROM processed_events WHERE key = ?", key):
        return                                # re-delivery is normal, not an error
    # Provider dedupes on the key across the ambiguous timeout window
    gateway.charge(event.amount, event.token, idempotency_key=key)
    # Unique index on key is the real guard against concurrent duplicates
    db.run("INSERT INTO processed_events (key) VALUES (?)", key)
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced at the storage and protocol layers, not by careful code:

- **Idempotency keys at the API edge**: the gateway rejects unsafe-method calls without an Idempotency-Key header and replays the stored first response for duplicates.
- **Unique constraints as the last line of defense**: a natural key (event ID, order ID) with a unique index; INSERT with conflict handling instead of check-then-write races.
- **Consumer-side dedupe**: dedupe on message identity before any side effect runs, regardless of broker guarantees.
- **Run markers for scripts**: every mutating job records a completed marker; re-running a completed job is a logged no-op.
- **Replay tests in CI**: re-deliver every message in a fixture set a second time and diff the final state — the diff must be empty.

## Real-world case

(ilustratif) A checkout service calls its payment provider with no idempotency key. Under load, the provider call times out for sixty seconds; the client retry policy fires three times per request; every retry lands once the provider recovers. Customers are double- and triple-charged, support tickets and manual reconciliation follow, and finance loses days. One stable key per order would have reduced the whole event to a cached first response. (verification: perlu — real double-charge incidents exist in public postmortems; belum digali — read the specific sources before citing any of them.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Safety vs. latency**: key lookups and dedupe tables add milliseconds to every write; they remove entire classes of incident. Pay the milliseconds.
- **Idempotency vs. Retry Budget**: retries are only legitimate on idempotent operations; sequence the two principles — make the operation safe, then budget the retries.
- **Idempotency vs. intent**: keys scoped too broadly (per customer instead of per order) silently block legitimate repeat purchases. Scope keys to the operation's natural identity, not to the actor.

## Related principles

- [Retry Budget](/docs/principles/reliability/retry-budget) — retries amplify load; only affordable where idempotency holds.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — bounds one bad action; idempotency bounds one repeated action.
- [Append-Only Logs](/docs/principles/data/append-only-logs) — stable event IDs make replay and dedupe natural.
- [Fail-Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — a dedupe miss must surface loudly, not corrupt silently.

## References

- Waldo et al., *A Note on Distributed Computing*, 1994 — partial failure means you cannot know whether the callee executed; idempotency makes that ambiguity survivable (verification: perlu — confirm framing before quoting).
- Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2017 — idempotence as the foundation of effectively-once processing (verification: perlu).

---

# Category: testing

## Property-Based Testing
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/testing/property-based-testing
- Category: testing · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: State the invariants your code must hold for every input, then let a generator hunt for the inputs that break them — one property beats a shelf of hand-picked examples.
> Stop enumerating example inputs by hand. For any behavior with a real invariant — round-trips, ordering, idempotence, commutativity — state the invariant as a property and let a generator search for violating inputs; when one is found, keep the shrunk counterexample as a named regression test. Always inspect what the generator actually produces, so the search reaches the corners you care about instead of sampling the boring middle.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

An example test asserts the output for one input you thought of; a property asserts an invariant that must hold for every input a generator can produce. Property-based testing — introduced by Claessen and Hughes in QuickCheck (ICFP 2000) — expresses properties in the language of the program, tests them on large numbers of randomly generated cases, and reports a counterexample when one fails; modern implementations shrink failures toward a minimal reproducing input. The lineage runs from Haskell's QuickCheck through the Erlang version that Hughes co-founded Quviq to commercialize in 2006, to ports such as fast-check for JavaScript and TypeScript and Hypothesis for Python. The shift in posture is the point: examples verify the cases you imagined, properties attack the case space you did not.

## When to use

- Pure logic with crisp invariants: codecs and serializers (round-trip), parsers (print-parse identity), collections (order, size, membership), money and date arithmetic.
- Input domains too wide to enumerate: unicode, negative and boundary numbers, empty and singleton cases, deeply nested structures.
- Regression discipline: every field-reported bug becomes a property plus its failing seed, so the search keeps covering that class of failure, not just the one reported case.
- Stateful systems where the interesting failures are interleavings: generated command sequences exploring states that hand-written tests never guess.

## When NOT to use

- Behavior specified by exact content — snapshot tests, golden files, copy text: the example is the contract, and a property adds no authority over it.
- Logic with no statable invariant: if you cannot say what always holds, the problem is an unwritten contract (see Explicit Contracts), not a missing generator.
- Slow side-effectful flows: generation multiplies executions; keep properties near pure logic and cover the I/O seams with a few focused integration tests.
- Once-and-discarded scripts whose entire input space is one file you control.

## Anti-pattern

- Tautology properties that restate the implementation — testing one function by computing the other side of the equality the same way the code does.
- Trivially true properties ("output is not null") that inflate the suite's greenness while constraining nothing.
- Unconstrained generators that produce mostly invalid inputs, so the run budget is spent on cases the precondition skips.
- Never inspecting the generator's distribution — the suite passes while sampling only the easy middle of the input space.
- Discarding the failing seed: a counterexample nobody can reproduce is a bug report without an address.
- Treating shrinking as optional — an unshrunk failure buries the actual trigger somewhere inside a screenful of random data.

## Code example

Wrong — three examples, all from the top of the author's head:

```ts
// urlCodec: decode(encode(s)) is supposed to be the identity.
test('encodes a path', () => {
  expect(decode(encode('users/42'))).toBe('users/42');
});
test('encodes a space', () => {
  expect(decode(encode('new york'))).toBe('new york');
});
test('encodes an accent', () => {
  expect(decode(encode('café'))).toBe('café');
});
// Input space actually tested: three strings. Multi-byte boundaries,
// percent signs, empty input, control characters — never generated,
// never tested. The first caller who produces one files a ticket.
```

Right — the invariant as a property, with the shrink kept as a regression:

```ts
import fc from 'fast-check';

// The invariant: decode after encode is the identity, for ANY string.
test('round-trips every generated string', () => {
  fc.assert(
    fc.property(fc.string(), (s) => {
      expect(decode(encode(s))).toBe(s);
    }),
    { numRuns: 2000 }, // budget the runs deliberately, not by accident of a default
  );
});

// On failure the runner prints the seed and the shrunk counterexample,
// e.g. "Property failed after 12 tests (seed: 1527422598337)".
// Pin that case by name so the bug class stays dead:
test('regression: percent sign survives the round-trip', () => {
  expect(decode(encode('%'))).toBe('%');
});
```

## Technical enforcement

Generation must be governed, not just admired:

- **Seed discipline**: every CI run records the seed the runner prints on failure; a property failure without a reproducible seed is treated as a broken test, not a green one.
- **Counterexample-to-regression gate**: a failing property must land as a named, checked-in regression test in the same PR as its fix — the shrunk case itself, not a paraphrase of it.
- **Distribution checks**: generators label their output categories, and the suite fails when a label disappears — the search cannot silently retreat to the easy middle.
- **Runtime budget**: property suites get an explicit time budget in CI with a loud signal when it is exceeded, so generation does not quietly rot the build's duration.
- **Tautology review**: properties that mirror the implementation under test are rejected in review exactly like assertions that assert nothing.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: distribution gates and run budgets prevent vacuous suites; seed logs and shrunk regressions detect the bugs the search has already found. Both halves, always.

## Real-world case

John Hughes — co-author of the original QuickCheck paper — recounts a decade of industrial results in "Experiences with QuickCheck: Testing the Hard Stuff and Staying Sane". The largest QuickCheck project to date, as of that writing, built acceptance tests for AUTOSAR C code on behalf of Volvo Cars, and a QuickCheck race-detection method "nailed a notorious bug plaguing Klarna", northern Europe's market leader in invoicing systems for e-commerce. Both are the same posture at industrial scale: invariants stated as executable properties, an input space explored by generator, and stateful interleavings attacked with generated sequences rather than hand-guessed ones. https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-30936-1_9 (verification: ok — facts quoted from the chapter's abstract; the Klarna bug mechanics and project detail live in the chapter body — belum digali, the full text is paywalled.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Breadth vs. determinism**: random inputs make every run a new experiment; without recorded seeds, a failing property is indistinguishable from a flaky test — the discipline of Flaky Test Quarantine is the price of the breadth.
- **Properties vs. examples**: a property surviving thousands of generated inputs still does not prove the invariant, and it documents nothing about intent; keep the handful of examples that explain the behavior and let generation hunt between them — the same fast-slow split the Test Pyramid prescribes, applied inside one suite.
- **Contract vs. mirror**: the strongest properties state the contract users depend on; the weakest restate the implementation and fail only when the code is rearranged — the line Test Behavior, Not Implementation draws for example tests, drawn sharper here.

## Related principles

- [Test Behavior, Not Implementation](/docs/principles/testing/test-behavior-not-implementation) — a property is the sharpest tool for pinning observable behavior instead of structure.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — a statable property is a contract made executable; an unstatable one is a missing contract.
- [Test Pyramid](/docs/principles/testing/test-pyramid) — where fast generated suites sit relative to slow integration coverage.
- [Flaky Test Quarantine](/docs/principles/testing/flaky-test-quarantine) — an unrecorded seed is a flaky test in embryo.

## References

- Claessen & Hughes, *QuickCheck: A Lightweight Tool for Random Testing of Haskell Programs*, ICFP 2000 — https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/john-hughes/quick.pdf (the original paper: properties as functions, random cases, custom generators.)
- John Hughes, *Experiences with QuickCheck: Testing the Hard Stuff and Staying Sane*, Springer 2016 — https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-30936-1_9 (industrial QuickCheck: Volvo Cars AUTOSAR acceptance tests, the Klarna race bug.)
- fast-check documentation — https://fast-check.dev/ (property-based testing for JavaScript and TypeScript: runners, arbitraries, shrinking.)
- Hypothesis documentation — https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/ (the property-based testing library for Python.)

## Don't Mock What You Don't Own
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/testing/dont-mock-what-you-dont-own
- Category: testing · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Never hand-write mocks of a third-party SDK's interface — wrap it in an adapter you own, double the adapter in fast tests, and verify the adapter against the real service.
> When a test needs to isolate code from a third-party SDK, client, or API, never hand-write a mock of the vendor's interface — you are guessing at someone else's semantics and grading yourself on the guess. Wrap the dependency once in a thin adapter whose interface you own, double that adapter in fast tests, and keep a small set of tests that exercise the adapter against the real service or its sanctioned sandbox. If a test starts spelling out a vendor's method names, move the boundary instead.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

A mock encodes assumptions about behavior you did not write, cannot change, and usually have not read. The rule is the community's distillation of the mock-objects school behind Freeman and Pryce's *Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests* — and their earlier OOPSLA paper states the core directly: mock objects turned out to be "less interesting as a technique for isolating tests from third-party libraries than is widely thought". The working form: double roles and interfaces you own, and treat every external service as an architectural boundary. Wrap it in an adapter whose interface is yours — names, errors, and semantics you chose — double that port in unit tests, and verify the one adapter against the real thing, so the vendor's quirks and evolution live in exactly one small place instead of being re-guessed in every test file.

## When to use

- Any unit test tempted to stub a vendor SDK's client, transport, or internals.
- Dependencies that version aggressively, where breaking changes arrive between minor releases.
- Infrastructure clients — payments, mail, storage, SMS, identity — where a wrong assumption means a production failure with a green suite behind it.
- Fast feedback loops that cannot afford real network calls on every run.

## When NOT to use

- Interfaces you own: double them freely — driving out your own roles with test doubles is the technique working as designed.
- A dependency you use trivially and unchanged, where one integration test costs less than maintaining a wrapper layer indefinitely.
- Providers that maintain an official, first-party test double with documented fidelity guarantees — that double is part of the provider's contract, not your guess about it.
- Exploratory spikes against a service you have not committed to; delete or vet them before anything ships.

## Anti-pattern

- Patching the vendor module in the test runner and inventing response objects from its type signatures — method names guessed, error shapes imagined, pagination semantics unknown.
- Mocking private or internal classes via reflection to force exotic error paths the public API never promises.
- A suite that never once talks to the real service until production traffic does.
- Replaying a response copied from production, then hand-editing it until the assertions pass — a mock of a guess of a memory.
- Upgrading a vendor major version by patching the mocks until green, without a single check against the real surface.

## Code example

Wrong — mocking the vendor's interface directly:

```ts
import { PaymentSDK } from 'vendor-payments'; // third-party SDK — not ours

jest.mock('vendor-payments');
// A hand-built fake of someone else's interface: names guessed from docs,
// error shapes invented, idempotency semantics unknown to its author.
const sdk = jest.mocked(PaymentSDK);
sdk.charge.mockResolvedValue({ ok: true });               // does the real one say ok?
sdk.charge.mockRejectedValue(new Error('card_declined')); // is that its error type?

test('checkout charges the customer', async () => {
  await checkout(user, 42);
  expect(sdk.charge).toHaveBeenCalled(); // proves our guess, not the vendor
});
```

Right — own the boundary, double the port, verify the adapter:

```ts
// payments.ts — the boundary is OURS: names, errors, and semantics we chose.
export interface PaymentGateway {
  charge(amountCents: number, token: string):
    Promise<{ id: string } | { declined: true }>;
}

// Fast unit test: the double stands in for OUR port, not their SDK.
test('a declined card creates no order', async () => {
  const gateway: PaymentGateway = { charge: async () => ({ declined: true }) };
  await expect(checkout(user, 42, gateway)).rejects.toThrow(PaymentDeclined);
});

// Adapter test: the ONE place the vendor SDK is real (sandbox or recorded
// traffic). Vendor drift breaks HERE, in CI, not in production.
test('adapter maps vendor failures onto our contract', async () => {
  const gateway = new VendorPaymentGateway(SANDBOX_KEY);
  const result = await gateway.charge(42, 'tok_charge_declined');
  expect(result).toEqual({ declined: true });
});
```

## Technical enforcement

The rule is only real when the build enforces the boundary:

- **Import restrictions**: lint rules forbid importing vendor SDKs outside their adapter module — "only the adapter touches the vendor" becomes machine-checked, not tribal memory.
- **Contract tests on adapters**: every adapter carries at least one test against the real service or its sanctioned sandbox in a labeled CI job, so vendor drift surfaces as a red build rather than a production page.
- **Double review rule**: hand-written doubles of third-party interfaces are review blockers; the reviewer's first question is "whose interface is this double describing?".
- **Recorded traffic over invented payloads**: when real calls are too costly for CI, replay recorded interactions with an expiry date — recordings expire and force a re-capture; fiction does not.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: import restrictions prevent new mocks of interfaces you do not own; sandbox contract tests detect the vendor moving underneath the adapter. Both halves, always.

## Real-world case

A March 2024 bug report against LocalStack — a widely used stand-in for AWS in tests — documents the failure mode with unusual precision. A developer switched a Lambda's DynamoDB access from Query to BatchGet but forgot to change the IAM permission from dynamodb:Query to dynamodb:BatchGetItem. Every test run against LocalStack passed, because the emulator does not enforce DynamoDB action permissions; the missing permission surfaced only when the code ran against real AWS, as a permission error. The reporter's own closing expectation: "My expectation was this would have been caught in localstack." https://github.com/localstack/localstack/issues/10517 (verification: ok — issue text quoted; what failed downstream in production beyond the reported AWS error is not described — belum digali.) A check at the real boundary, even a thin one, would have surfaced the policy mismatch earlier — as a failing pipeline step instead of a runtime permission error.

## Tension and trade-off

- **Speed vs. fidelity**: a suite of doubles is fast and quiet exactly where it is lying; the Test Pyramid's answer is a thin base of real-boundary tests so vendor drift is caught somewhere cheap.
- **Wrapper cost vs. direct dependency**: every adapter is code you now own and maintain; Dependency Inversion earns its keep only where the boundary is real — wrapping a dependency you use trivially trades one liability for another.
- **Your contract vs. vendor drift**: even through an adapter you will come to depend on vendor behavior nobody documented — Hyrum's Law works on providers too; adapter contract tests are how that silent dependence gets noticed.

## Related principles

- [Test Behavior, Not Implementation](/docs/principles/testing/test-behavior-not-implementation) — mocking a vendor's internals couples your suite to their implementation choices.
- [Dependency Inversion](/docs/principles/architecture/dependency-inversion) — the adapter is the abstraction you depend on instead of the SDK.
- [Test Pyramid](/docs/principles/testing/test-pyramid) — the thin real-boundary base that keeps doubles honest.
- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — undocumented vendor behavior becomes your dependency whether you noticed or not.

## References

- Freeman & Pryce, *Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests* (2009) — https://growing-object-oriented-software.com/ (the book's home: TDD with mock objects driving design at boundaries you own; verification: ok for the book and site, perlu for whether the five-word phrase appears verbatim in the text — belum digali.)
- Freeman, Pryce, Mackinnon & Walnes, *Mock Roles, not Objects*, OOPSLA 2004 — https://jmock.org/oopsla2004.pdf (mock objects as a design technique, and the paper's own verdict on isolating third-party libraries.)
- Martin Fowler, *Mocks Aren't Stubs* — https://martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html (the vocabulary of test doubles and the classical vs. mockist distinction.)
