## Test Pyramid
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/testing/test-pyramid
- Category: testing · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Balance the automated test suite by feedback cost — many fast unit tests, some integration tests, few end-to-end tests.
> Shape every automated test suite as a pyramid: many small and fast unit tests at the base, a thinner layer of integration tests, and only a few slow end-to-end tests at the top. Push each assertion down to the lowest layer that can still observe the behavior it cares about, and treat a suite that takes hours to run as a defect in the suite, not a fact of life. Never answer a slow, flaky suite by adding more tests at the top — go down a layer instead.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

The test pyramid — coined by Mike Cohn in Succeeding with Agile and popularized by Ham Vocke's "The Practical Test Pyramid" — is a metaphor for a balanced suite: lots of small and fast unit tests, some more coarse-grained integration tests, very few high-level end-to-end tests. The shape encodes cost: tests higher up the stack are slower, flakier, and harder to diagnose when they fail, so the suite buys coverage where tests are cheap to run and cheap to fix, and reserves the expensive top for the journeys that genuinely need the whole system wired together. What the shape buys is feedback speed — automation should tell you the software is broken "in a matter of seconds and minutes instead of days and weeks". Vocke's warning about the inverted shape, the "test ice-cream cone", is that it "will be a nightmare to maintain and takes way too long to run".

## When to use

- Any codebase whose CI test runtime gates merges or releases.
- Teams practicing continuous integration, where the feedback loop has to survive merging many times a day.
- Service and library code whose logic can be exercised without a full deployment.
- Rescuing a suite developers have stopped running locally because it takes too long.

## When NOT to use

- Throwaway spikes and prototypes that will never reach production — a testing strategy for code with a lifespan of days is noise.
- Safety-critical or contractually regulated paths that require end-to-end evidence: the top of the pyramid is budgeted by risk, not by taste.
- Hard-to-test legacy systems where the wiring itself is the risk — pin current behavior first (see Legacy Code Is Untested Code) before enforcing layer shapes.
- Front-end codebases whose tooling has made integration tests nearly as fast as unit tests — optimize for return on investment over shape (Dodds' Testing Trophy).

## Anti-pattern

- The ice-cream cone: a mountain of end-to-end UI tests over a thin base of unit tests — slow, flaky, and it diagnoses nothing.
- Testing every business rule through the full stack: forty seconds of login, database, and browser to learn one number.
- Fighting about layer names ("is that a unit test?") instead of asking what a test observes and how fast it runs — Vocke explicitly warns not to get attached to the names of the layers.
- Mandating layer ratios or coverage percentages per repository — the pyramid is a cost heuristic, and Goodhart's Law will collect the metric.
- A suite so slow that developers batch changes around overnight runs and read the results the next morning.

## Code example

Wrong — one business rule, tested only through the whole browser:

```ts
// e2e/checkout.spec.ts — the ONLY test covering the volume-discount rule
test('volume discount', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.fill('#email', 'e2e-bot@example.com'); // full stack for one rule:
  await page.click('#login');                        // auth, session, database
  for (let i = 0; i < 11; i++) {
    await page.click('#add-to-cart');                // 11 browser round-trips
  }
  await expect(page.locator('#total')).toHaveText('104.50'); // ~40s of setup
});
```

Right — the rule as a fast unit test, the journey as one smoke test:

```ts
// unit/discount.spec.ts — the rule itself, in milliseconds
test('11th item is free', () => {
  const cart = items(11, unitPrice(9.5));
  expect(volumeDiscount(cart)).toBe(104.5); // 10 paid, 1 free
});

// e2e/checkout.smoke.spec.ts — exactly ONE journey proves the wiring
// (login, add one item, see a plausible total); it does not re-prove
// rules the unit layer already owns.
```

## Technical enforcement

The pyramid itself is advice about where assertions live; the pipeline enforces its consequences:

- **CI runtime budget**: the default merge-gating suite has a hard runtime cap; exceeding it fails the build and forces new tests down a layer or into a scheduled lane.
- **Layer tagging**: every test declares its layer; CI reports per-layer runtime and counts as a trend, so an inverting pyramid becomes visible instead of ambient.
- **Merge gate on the fast lane**: pull requests are gated on unit and integration tests; end-to-end suites run post-merge or on a schedule, with loud reporting back into the backlog.
- **End-to-end quota in review**: a change that adds end-to-end tests must justify why the assertion cannot live lower — as a required review checklist item.
- **Per-layer flake tracking**: failures are attributed to layers; a layer whose failures are mostly flaky gets quarantine treatment (see Flaky Test Quarantine), not more tests.

## Real-world case

Google's testing blog argued the economics from practice in "Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests" (Mike Wacker, April 2015). https://testing.googleblog.com/2015/04/just-say-no-to-more-end-to-end-tests.html Wacker presents what he explicitly labels a composite sketch, based on a collection of real experiences: a team gates its release on a nightly end-to-end suite, and with one day to the deadline the pass rate collapses — first because signing in to the service is broken and almost all tests sign in a user, then again because a partner team deployed a bad build to the shared testing environment. The article's conclusion is the pyramid's argument in production terms: smaller tests are fast ("no developer wants to wait hours or days to find out if their change works") and reliable, while a strategy built mostly on end-to-end tests turns every small defect into a suite-wide event. A lower-layer suite would have reduced the blast radius of each of those defects to one failing test with one obvious cause.

## Tension and trade-off

- **Test Pyramid vs. Testing Trophy**: when integration tests are nearly as fast as unit tests (much modern front-end tooling), shape stops being the point — Kent C. Dodds proposes weighting layers by return on investment instead of by count.
- **Fast lane vs. real wiring**: gating merges on the fast lane alone means integration defects surface only after merge; pair the schedule with Fail-Visible reporting so the post-merge lane alarms instead of whispering.
- **Weigh against Goodhart's Law**: the moment the pyramid is enforced as layer ratios or coverage numbers, the metric gets gamed and the cost heuristic behind it is forgotten.

## Related principles

- [Test Behavior, Not Implementation](/docs/principles/testing/test-behavior-not-implementation) — the fast base layer is only an asset if the small tests observe behavior, not call graphs.
- [Flaky Test Quarantine](/docs/principles/testing/flaky-test-quarantine) — top-heavy suites are where flakiness breeds; contain it deliberately.
- [Fail Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — exceeded runtime budgets and post-merge failures must be loud, not ambient.
- [Goodhart's Law](/docs/principles/design/goodharts-law) — layer ratios and coverage percentages become targets the moment they are measured as targets.

## References

- Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid — https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html (layering, what to test at each level, the ice-cream-cone anti-pattern; attributes the concept to Mike Cohn's Succeeding with Agile).
- Kent C. Dodds, Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration. — https://kentcdodds.com/blog/write-tests (the Testing Trophy — weighting layers by return on investment when integration tests are cheap).
- Mike Wacker, Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests — https://testing.googleblog.com/2015/04/just-say-no-to-more-end-to-end-tests.html (why end-to-end-heavy strategies fail in practice: slow, flaky, hard to diagnose).

---

## Flaky Test Quarantine
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/testing/flaky-test-quarantine
- Category: testing · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: A test that fails intermittently on unchanged code poisons trust in the whole suite — isolate it deliberately, with a bug and an expiry, instead of rerunning until green.
> Treat a test that fails intermittently on unchanged code as a defect with a deadline, not as noise to be rerun. Quarantine it out of the critical path, attach a tracking bug, and set an expiry after which the quarantine itself fails the build. Never auto-rerun failures until green and never delete the test silently — a quarantine that decays invisibly becomes a blind spot that hides real races.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

A flaky test exhibits both passing and failing results with the same code — Google's own definition, from John Micco's 2016 testing-blog post. Flakiness destroys the suite's core product: trust. Once engineers learn that red can mean "try again", they stop reading failures — including the real ones — and Micco's numbers show the scale at Google: about 1.5% of all test runs report a flaky result, almost 16% of tests carry some level of flakiness, and the insertion rate of flaky tests has roughly matched the fix rate despite dedicated effort. Quarantine is the containment practice: the flaky test is removed from the critical path, a bug is filed to fix it, and the quarantine itself is tracked — with an owner and an expiry — so containment can never quietly become a permanent hole in coverage.

## When to use

- Any CI suite gating merges or releases where intermittent failures have been observed more than once.
- Large test corpora run continuously — flakiness grows with suite size and with the share of end-to-end tests.
- Teams whose developers have started saying "just rerun it": the trust damage has already begun.
- Workflows with a build cop or human triaging failures, where every flake costs investigation time.

## When NOT to use

- When the failure is deterministic and reproducible — that is an ordinary failing test; fix the code, do not label it.
- Flakiness caused by a race in the production code under test — that is a product bug traveling through the test; surface it, do not quarantine it.
- Small suites where the flaky test can simply be fixed now — quarantine exists for when fix throughput cannot keep pace with arrivals.
- As a response to a single unexplained failure: without measured pass/fail variance, "flaky" is a guess, and the guess can bury a real regression.

## Anti-pattern

- Auto-rerunning failed tests until they pass, with no record kept — every flake becomes invisible, and each silent rerun widens the blind spot.
- A drive-by skip annotation on the flaky test: coverage vanishes with no bug, no decision, and no trace.
- "Flaky" as a personal verdict — any developer may declare red to be noise at discretion, and the verdict decays into red-is-ignorable.
- A quarantine list nobody reviews: the test is out of the critical path and out of everyone's mind, forever.
- Blaming the toolchain ("the runners were slow yesterday") instead of measuring per-test pass/fail variance.

## Code example

Wrong — rerun until green:

```python
# run_tests.py — the classic: failures vanish by retry, no record kept
import subprocess

code = 1
for _ in range(3):  # a test failing 2 of 3 runs now "passes"
    code = subprocess.call(["pytest", "-x", "--lf"])
    if code == 0:
        break
raise SystemExit(code)  # the flake was never counted or owned
```

Right — explicit quarantine with bug and expiry:

```python
# run_tests.py — the suite stays deterministic; known-flaky tests are
# quarantined by name, each with a tracking bug and an expiry date.
import datetime
import subprocess

QUARANTINE = {
    "tests/test_webhook.py::test_retry_on_timeout": {
        "bug": "PLAT-1423",  # why it is flaky, tracked where work lives
        "expires": datetime.date(2026, 9, 30),  # quarantine is temporary
    },
}

stale = [t for t, meta in QUARANTINE.items()
         if meta["expires"] <= datetime.date.today()]
if stale:
    # the quarantine rots loudly: expired entries fail the build
    raise SystemExit(f"quarantine expired - fix or re-triage: {stale}")

subprocess.call(["pytest", "-m", "not quarantined"])
```

## Technical enforcement

Quarantine is a workflow, and the workflow can be made mechanical:

- **Automatic flake detection**: CI records per-test pass/fail variance across runs on unchanged code; a test crossing a configured flakiness threshold is flagged, and optionally auto-quarantined — the tool Google describes does exactly this.
- **Quarantine registry as data**: quarantined tests live in a checked-in registry, each entry carrying a bug link and an expiry; registry changes are reviewed like any other diff.
- **Expiry gates the build**: expired entries fail CI until the test is fixed, re-triaged, or deleted with an explicit decision — containment never becomes permanent by neglect.
- **No silent retries**: automatic rerun of failures is either disabled or emits a per-test counter; a rising retry count is itself a quarantine trigger.
- **Quarantine dashboard**: flaky count, entry age, and coverage lost to quarantine are reported to the team, so the debt stays visible instead of ambient.

## Real-world case

Google described the practice publicly in John Micco's "Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them" (May 2016). https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html Across Google's corpus, about 1.5% of all test runs report a flaky result — defined there as a test "that exhibits both a passing and a failing result with the same code" — and almost 16% of tests carry some level of flakiness; with an average project of roughly a thousand tests, the arithmetic alone produces a steady stream of false alarms per run, each requiring investigation by a developer or build cop. One published mitigation is a tool that monitors flakiness and automatically quarantines a test when it is too high: quarantine removes the test from the critical path and files a bug for developers to reduce the flakiness. Micco's own caveat is this principle's tension: quarantine "could easily mask a real race condition or some other bug in the code being tested", and the softer alternative — marking a test flaky so it fails only after three consecutive failures — delays a real breakage in a fifteen-minute test to roughly forty-five minutes. The published menu (rerun, mark-as-flaky, quarantine-with-bug) is exactly the policy surface this principle formalizes: contain the noise, keep the debt visible, and never let containment become the fix.

## Tension and trade-off

- **Quarantine vs. Fail-Visible**: moving a flaky test out of the critical path trades signal for stability — the failure still exists, only somewhere quieter; keep the registry loud or the mask becomes permanent.
- **Auto-rerun vs. Retry Budget**: rerunning failed tests until green is a retry loop with no budget — it spends build time to buy an illusion; if retries exist at all, they are capped, counted, and reported like any other retry.
- **Weigh against Observability First**: the flake may be the only witness of a real race or ordering bug — treat per-test variance as telemetry about production behavior, not just as suite debt.

## Related principles

- [Test Pyramid](/docs/principles/testing/test-pyramid) — top-heavy suites are the main generator of flakiness; fewer, lower tests is the structural fix.
- [Fail Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — an expired or growing quarantine must alarm, not dissolve into the background.
- [Retry Budget](/docs/principles/reliability/retry-budget) — auto-rerun is a retry: bounded, counted, and reported, or not at all.
- [Observability First](/docs/principles/reliability/observability-first) — per-test pass/fail variance is telemetry about the code, not only about the suite.

## References

- John Micco, Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them — https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html (Google's flakiness rates and mitigation tools: rerun failing tests, mark-as-flaky, automatic quarantine with filed bugs).
- Mike Wacker, Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests — https://testing.googleblog.com/2015/04/just-say-no-to-more-end-to-end-tests.html (why flaky tests erode developer trust, and why smaller tests are the reliable base).

---

## Test Behavior, Not Implementation
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/testing/test-behavior-not-implementation
- Category: testing · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Assert what the system does — observable states and effects — not how it does it; tests coupled to internal call graphs break on every safe refactor.
> Write tests that assert observable outcomes — returned values, state changes, effects sent to the world — instead of asserting which collaborators were called, in what order, with which arguments. Prefer real, fast collaborators (in-memory repositories, capture adapters) over call-sequence mocks, and reserve interaction assertions for interactions that are themselves the contract. When a refactor with identical observable behavior breaks your tests, fix the tests — not the refactor.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

A useful test fails when behavior changes and passes when it does not. The mockist (London-school) style verifies interactions — which collaborator was called, in what order, with what arguments — which couples the test to the implementation's call graph; the classical (Detroit-school) style verifies state and effects through real collaborators and stays blind to internal structure. Martin Fowler's "Mocks Aren't Stubs" (2007) documents both styles and their names — Detroit for classical, London for mockist, after the places the XP communities grew up — and states the cost plainly: mockist tests are "more coupled to the implementation of a method", and "changing the nature of calls to collaborators usually cause a mockist test to break" even when nothing observable changed. Testing behavior, not implementation, is what keeps a suite a refactoring safety net — which is the only durable reason to have one.

## When to use

- Code under active refactoring, where the suite is the safety net that makes change cheap.
- Test-driven development at the unit level: test the next observable behavior, then let the implementation emerge.
- Shared libraries and internal services, where collaborators' call sequences are part of nobody's contract.
- Teams adopting mocking frameworks, deciding what to assert before writing the first mock.

## When NOT to use

- When the interaction is the specification — "the payment provider must be charged exactly once", "the audit event must be emitted before the state flips": asserting that interaction is behavior, not implementation leakage.
- Boundary adapters at the edge of the system, where the bytes on the wire (event schema, header, encoding) are the contract consumers parse — verify the wire, not the object graph.
- Third-party collaborators you do not own — do not mock their internals at all; wrap them and test the wrapper (see Don't Mock What You Don't Own).
- Legacy code with no seams: pin current behavior with characterization tests first (see Legacy Code Is Untested Code), before judging any test's style.

## Anti-pattern

- A mock asserting a precise call sequence between two internal collaborators — the test now fails on every rename.
- Deep-equality assertions on entire argument objects when one field is the behavior and the rest is incidental.
- A "refactor" that consists of editing forty mocks until they match the new internal call structure, approved by tests that never asked what the system does.
- Coverage built mostly from call-assertions: a green suite with no opinion about whether outcomes are right.
- Mocking value objects and pure functions that could simply be run.

## Code example

Wrong — the test pins the call graph:

```ts
test('order placement', () => {
  const repo = mock();
  const mailer = mock();
  const svc = new OrderService(repo, mailer);

  svc.place(cart);

  expect(repo.save).toHaveBeenCalledWithExactly(expectedOrder); // exact record
  expect(mailer.send).toHaveBeenCalledBefore(repo.save); // internal ordering
});
// Renaming repo.save to repo.persist, or sending the receipt after saving
// (no observable change), breaks this test: the safety net is gone.
```

Right — the test asserts state and effects:

```ts
test('placing an order persists it and sends exactly one receipt', () => {
  const repo = new InMemoryOrderRepo(); // real, fast collaborator
  const mailer = new CaptureMailer(); // captures what was sent, not who called

  new OrderService(repo, mailer).place(cart);

  expect(repo.findByUser(cart.userId)).toHaveLength(1); // state: order exists
  expect(mailer.sent.map((m) => m.to)).toEqual([cart.email]); // one receipt
});
// Internal names, ordering, and call structure can now change freely;
// the test fails only when the behavior it names actually changes.
```

## Technical enforcement

Style cannot be held by review alone; wire the constraint into the tooling:

- **Mock allowlists**: the mocking configuration permits test doubles only for collaborators at architectural boundaries; doubling a deep-internal seam requires an explicit, reviewed exception.
- **Interaction assertions carry a marker**: assertions that verify calls must sit in files tagged as contract tests, or CI annotates them for review before merge.
- **Mutation testing**: mutants that survive reveal tests asserting structure instead of outcomes; track the per-module survival trend.
- **Refactor drill in CI**: a scheduled job applies behavior-preserving transformations (renames, reordering of independent calls) and requires the suite to stay green — coupling shows up as failures on a no-op change.
- **Enforcement vs. detection**: allowlists and markers stop new coupling at review; mutation testing and refactor drills detect the coupling you already have — run both halves.

## Real-world case

(ilustratif) A team renames a persistence method and reorders two internal steps — save the order, then send the receipt — with no observable change: the same data is stored, the same email is delivered. The mock-based suite fails across dozens of tests asserting the old method name and the old ordering; a developer spends the afternoon rewriting mocks to match the new call structure, and the change is "approved" by tests that never once asked what the system does. The suite's value as a safety net erodes quietly until a genuine behavior change slips through the same just-fix-the-mocks reflex. Behavior-level assertions would have reduced that entire class of failure to a green build and a one-line rename. (verification: perlu — the coupling mechanism is documented in Fowler's "Mocks Aren't Stubs"; belum digali — a named public account of a behavior-preserving refactor breaking a mock-based suite has not been verified yet.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Classical vs. mockist (Detroit vs. London)**: mockist tests pinpoint exactly which interaction broke; classical tests survive refactors but localize failures more coarsely — choose by how stable the design already is.
- **Behavior vs. explicit contracts**: when the interaction itself is the specification (charge exactly once, emit before flip), the interaction assertion is behavior — weigh against Explicit Contracts and write it as a contract test, not as an incidental mock.
- **Weigh against Test Pyramid**: classical tests need real collaborators, which pushes some assertions into slower layers — buy the speed back with in-memory fakes and capture adapters, not with call-graph mocks.

## Related principles

- [Don't Mock What You Don't Own](/docs/principles/testing/dont-mock-what-you-dont-own) — the sharpest form of implementation coupling: mocking the internals of a dependency you cannot change.
- [Test Pyramid](/docs/principles/testing/test-pyramid) — where behavior-level assertions live, layer by layer.
- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — an asserted call sequence becomes a contract the moment the green suite is depended on.
- [Legacy Code Is Untested Code](/docs/principles/testing/legacy-code-is-untested-code) — pin current behavior before refactoring; the safety-net argument only works when a net exists.

## References

The slogan "test behavior, not implementation" is community shorthand with no single canonical origin; this page anchors it to the documented debate below.

- Martin Fowler, Mocks Aren't Stubs — https://martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html (classical vs. mockist TDD, the Detroit and London names, and how mockist tests couple to implementation).
- Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid — https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html (sociable vs. solitary unit tests, and what to test at each layer).

---

## Legacy Code Is Untested Code
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/testing/legacy-code-is-untested-code
- Category: testing · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Code without fast tests is legacy the day it ships — you cannot change it safely, only guess. Pin what it actually does with characterization tests before touching a line.
> Treat any code without fast, reliable tests as legacy — including code written last sprint. Never refactor, clean up, or extend it blind: first pin its current behavior with characterization tests, warts included; then make your change with the pins green. If the code cannot be pinned because it is welded to I/O, open a seam and test through it — do not copy the logic out and fork it into two divergent versions, neither tested.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Michael Feathers' reframing, from *Working Effectively with Legacy Code* (2004), relocates "legacy" from age to risk: legacy code is code without tests — the definition is widely attributed to the book's introduction (verification: perlu for the exact sentence — the verbatim wording is belum digali; the book itself is billed as strategies for working with large, untested legacy code bases). The operational meaning: legacy code is code you are afraid to change. Without a safety net, every modification is archaeology plus hope; with one, refactoring becomes evidence work. Feathers' accompanying toolkit — characterization tests that assert what the code *does* do rather than what it should, and seams that make entangled code testable — is the mechanism that converts the fear into a green suite first and a safe change second.

## When to use

- Before any cleanup, refactor, or modernization PR in an area without fast tests.
- Before extending a long-lived module whose weird edge cases nobody can explain.
- Under emergency maintenance: pin the exact path you are about to touch — a narrow pin beats a blind hotfix.
- When inheriting or auditing a codebase: the tested part is the part that changes with evidence; the rest is legacy by definition, whatever its birth date.

## When NOT to use

- Code already held by fast tests: by this definition it is not legacy, however ugly — ugliness is a design judgment; fear is the legacy signal.
- Verified-dead code: delete it with evidence (see Chesterton's Fence) rather than pinning behavior nobody needs and carrying it forever.
- Code scheduled for replacement rather than modification — pinning what is about to be retired wastes the pin.
- As an excuse to skip understanding: a characterization test records behavior, it does not explain it; the fence's why still has to be hunted by hand.

## Anti-pattern

- "Rewrite it from scratch" as the reflex response to fear — the replacement inherits every unknown behavior while discarding years of quiet fixes.
- Cleaning up legacy inside a feature PR: behavior changes and intent changes share one diff, and neither can be reverted alone.
- Characterization tests written from the spec instead of observation — they fail against the real quirks, get deleted, and the code is right back to unpinned.
- Wrapping the whole module in one giant end-to-end test and calling it pinned — too slow to run constantly, too coarse to localize a slip.
- Copy-pasting legacy logic into a new module "with fixes", leaving two divergent copies, neither under test.

## Code example

Wrong — refactor without a pin:

```python
def apply_discount(order):
    # inherited logic: nobody remembers why over-100 goes through fees
    if order.total > 100 and order.coupon:
        return order.total * 0.9 - order.fees
    return order.total

# The "cleanup": someone deletes the fee subtraction because it looks
# wrong, and ships it. The customers whose bills that branch handled
# correctly-for-them find out in next month's invoices.
```

Right — pin observed behavior first, then change:

```python
def test_discount_over_100_with_coupon_is_pinned_as():
    # NOT what the code should do — what it observably DOES today.
    # If this pins a surprise, good: that surprise is exactly the
    # risk you were about to take blind.
    order = Order(total=120, coupon="SPRING", fees=5)
    assert apply_discount(order) == 103.0   # 120*0.9 - 5, warts included

def test_discount_below_100_ignores_coupon():
    order = Order(total=80, coupon="SPRING", fees=5)
    assert apply_discount(order) == 80      # no discount at all — pinned

# Pins green, behavior captured: now refactor apply_discount freely.
# Any behavioral slip becomes a red test before merge instead of a
# silent invoice error after it.
```

## Technical enforcement

Untested code must be expensive to touch, and the expense must be automatic:

- **Change-gated coverage**: CI fails a PR whose touched files lose fast-test coverage, or whose changed behavior paths carry no tests — the pin arrives with the change, never in a later sprint.
- **Untested-file inventory**: a generated report lists files with no fast tests; a diff touching them is flagged for characterization work automatically, not by memory.
- **Mutation spot-checks on new pins**: a light mutation run over newly pinned paths verifies the pins actually detect change — a pin that never fails is decoration, and the build treats it as such.
- **Separation-of-diff rule**: cleanup and behavior change in the same PR against unpinned code is a review blocker; the pinning diff lands first, on its own.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: change gates prevent new untested code from accumulating; the inventory and mutation checks detect how weak the existing pins are. Both halves, always.

## Real-world case

In April 2020, New Jersey's unemployment system — running on 40-year-old mainframes programmed in COBOL — met a pandemic surge: an unprecedented 362,000 people had applied for unemployment in the state, and its IT department was racing to keep the service running. Governor Phil Murphy publicly appealed for volunteer programmers who knew COBOL, and the state labor commissioner told reporters: "Literally, we have systems that are 40 years-plus old, and there'll be lots of postmortems." Maintaining your own production system by public appeal for volunteers is what "legacy code is untested code" looks like at state scale: code the owner cannot change with confidence, only staff. A characterization suite around the eligibility rules would not have absorbed the surge — it would have reduced the risk of the maintenance work the state's IT department was racing to do, on code nobody could afford to break. https://www.cnbc.com/2020/04/06/new-jersey-seeks-cobol-programmers-to-fix-unemployment-system.html (verification: ok for the quoted facts; the article does not describe the mainframes' test coverage — that the code was effectively unpinned is inference from era and appeal, tidak yakin; dig the postmortems the commissioner promised before quoting any.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Pinning cost vs. urgency**: emergencies do not wait for suites; the workable compromise is pinning exactly the paths about to change, not the whole module — the Test Pyramid's granularity logic applied to rescue work.
- **Observed behavior vs. intended spec**: characterization tests bless today's behavior, bugs included; each pinned wart must be a deliberate decision — preserve it, or change it knowingly — which is Test Behavior, Not Implementation taken to its honest extreme.
- **Refactor in place vs. rewrite**: fear of unpinned code pushes toward the big rewrite, but the replacement must itself grow from something working (Gall's Law), and the weird branches may carry reasons the pins will never reveal (Chesterton's Fence).

## Related principles

- [Test Behavior, Not Implementation](/docs/principles/testing/test-behavior-not-implementation) — characterization tests are the pure case: behavior as observed, never structure as designed.
- [Chesterton's Fence](/docs/principles/design/chesterton-fence) — a pin tells you what the fence does, never why it was built.
- [Gall's Law](/docs/principles/architecture/gall-law) — the counterweight to the rewrite reflex that fear of legacy induces.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — until pins exist, changes to legacy ship staged and revertable, because review alone cannot hold them.

## References

- Michael C. Feathers, *Working Effectively with Legacy Code* (2004) — https://www.informit.com/store/working-effectively-with-legacy-code-9780131177055 (the definition and the toolkit: characterization tests, seams, sprouting; verification: perlu for the verbatim sentence — sudah digali at the book-page level, the exact quote is belum digali.)
- CNBC, *New Jersey needs volunteers who know COBOL, a 60-year-old programming language* (April 2020) — https://www.cnbc.com/2020/04/06/new-jersey-seeks-cobol-programmers-to-fix-unemployment-system.html (the 40-year-old mainframes, the 362,000-application surge, the volunteer appeal, the commissioner's quote.)

# Category: api

## Robustness Principle
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/api/postel-robustness
- Category: api · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept — but write down exactly how liberal, or tolerance becomes unprovable behavior.
> Make your outputs conform exactly to the published contract — be strict on the sending side. On the receiving side, accept only the deviations you have written down, and reject everything else with a clear error. Log every tolerated deviation so tolerance stays observable. Never silently guess what malformed input meant.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

The Robustness Principle (RFC 1122, section 1.2.2) has two halves: implementations sending must be conservative — strictly conformant — while implementations receiving may be liberal, tolerating input that is imperfect but interpretable. The modern discipline adds a third clause: liberality must be bounded, documented, and observable. Tolerance that is neither written down nor logged is not robustness; it is an accident waiting to become someone else's dependency.

## When to use

- Public APIs and protocol endpoints serving many heterogeneous or legacy clients.
- Parsers for formats you do not control: email, feeds, CSV exports, third-party webhooks.
- Gateway or proxy layers that must keep imperfect partners working while the ecosystem cleans up.

## When NOT to use

- Parsing untrusted input where malformed data is an attack vector — strictness is the security posture here.
- Internal service meshes where you control both ends: strict rejection surfaces producer bugs at the earliest, cheapest moment.
- Anywhere tolerance would hide data corruption rather than inconvenience — a "liberally" accepted, wrong-but-parseable value that corrupts state is worse than a rejected request.

## Anti-pattern

- Accepting anything and guessing intent: a missing field defaults to some plausible value, unlogged.
- Silent coercion — the string "42" quietly becomes the number 42, and "abc" becomes 1.
- Being liberal in what you send because "the other side is also liberal".
- Tolerating deviations for years, then removing the tolerance with no version and no window.

## Code example

Wrong — accept anything, guess, and tell no one:

```ts
app.post('/orders', (req, res) => {
  const qty = Number(req.body.qty) || 1;   // "abc" silently becomes 1
  const note = req.body.note ?? '';        // null, undefined, false — all fine
  res.json({ ok: true, qty });            // shipped; nobody will ever know
});
```

Right — strict core, tolerance confined to one documented, logged case:

```ts
// Strict by default; ONE documented leniency (qty sent as numeric string)
const OrderIn = z.object({ qty: z.number().int().positive() }).strict();
app.post('/orders', (req, res) => {
  if (typeof req.body?.qty === 'string') {
    metrics.count('tolerated.qty_as_string'); // tolerance is observable
    req.body.qty = Number(req.body.qty);     // the one documented case
  }
  const parsed = OrderIn.safeParse(req.body);
  if (!parsed.success) return res.status(400).json(parsed.error.flatten());
  createOrder(parsed.data);                  // strict beyond the documented case
});
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced by schemas and tests, not by politeness:

- **Strict schemas at boundaries** (zod, JSON Schema, protobuf): unknown keys rejected, types exact — tolerance is an explicit, enumerated exception list in the schema or adapter.
- **Output conformance tests in CI**: golden tests asserting your responses match the published spec exactly — the conservative-sender half is testable.
- **Tolerance budget**: every accepted deviation gets a log line and a dashboard count; when the count stays at zero for a quarter, the tolerance becomes a deprecation candidate behind a version bump.
- **Fuzzing** the parser in CI to prove it rejects rather than improvises on malformed input.

## Real-world case

An API accepted ISO-style date strings and "helpfully" treated a missing timezone as UTC — for years, silently. A partner later started sending local-time timestamps; their stored records drifted by hours, and the corruption surfaced months later in reconciliation, with no trace of when or why the wrong interpretation happened, because the tolerance had never been logged. A strict parser would have surfaced the malformed dates the moment they arrived, instead of months later. (ilustratif — composite of a common failure mode; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **The modern critique — tolerance accumulates**: decades of liberal acceptance train an ecosystem where malformed output is de facto required (see Hyrum's Law), which is why strict protocol design argues receivers should reject and force producers to fix their bugs. Reserve tolerance for partners you cannot fix and for transitions you have scheduled.
- **Interoperability vs. security**: every accepted deviation is unvalidated surface area; for untrusted input, strictness wins on safety grounds.
- **Kindness vs. observability**: silent tolerance is kind today and unmaintainable tomorrow — the middle path is tolerate-and-log, then retire the tolerance through a versioned change.

## Related principles

- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — every tolerated deviation becomes somebody's dependency.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — what tolerance is allowed should live in the contract, not in code folklore.
- [Input Validation](/docs/principles/security/input-validation) — the strict counterpart at hostile boundaries.
- [Versioned Contracts](/docs/principles/api/versioned-contracts) — how to retire a tolerance without a rug pull.
- [Fail-Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — when rejection beats guessing.

## References

- RFC 1122, section 1.2.2 — the canonical statement: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122 (verified URL).
- Hyrum's Law — the dependency cost of unbounded tolerance: https://www.hyrumslaw.com (verified URL).

---

## Explicit Contracts
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts
- Category: api · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Everything crossing a boundary carries an explicit, validated contract — implicit assumptions rot silently until they fail at 3 a.m.
> Give every boundary crossing — HTTP request, queue message, webhook, database row, environment variable — a declared schema, and validate it at the point of entry. Treat any unwritten assumption (field order, nullability, units, timezone, encoding) as a defect waiting to be scheduled. If you consume a producer's output, insist on the schema in code and tests, not in folklore.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Every piece of data that crosses a process, service, or ownership boundary carries an explicit contract: a schema, owned and validated by the receiving side. Explicit means machine-checkable — a type in a shared package, a JSON Schema, a protobuf definition — not a wiki page. Implicit contracts (assumptions about ordering, formats, defaults) are still contracts; they are just unwitnessed, untested, and discovered in production.

## When to use

- Service-to-service and client-server calls; third-party webhooks and callbacks.
- Event streams and queues where producers and consumers deploy independently.
- Reading another team's tables, exports, or files — including the output of your own past migrations.
- Consuming configuration and environment variables at startup.

## When NOT to use

- Hot in-process calls already checked by the compiler — re-validating there is pure overhead; validate at the boundary, then trust types inside.
- One-off scripts over files you wrote and read in the same process.
- While a format is still being actively invented in a prototype — but promote it to a schema before a second consumer appears.

## Anti-pattern

- Positional unpacking of JSON fields — relying on undocumented order.
- "The producer always sends cents" or "the timestamp is always UTC" — nowhere written, nowhere checked.
- Copy-pasting a type into the consumer instead of sharing a versioned schema package.
- Schema drift: the producer evolves the payload, no diff fails, and the consumer's assumption quietly expires.

## Code example

Wrong — the contract lives in an undocumented assumption:

```ts
// "getJob always returns fields in insertion order" — said nobody, in writing, ever
const [id, status] = Object.values(await getJob(jobId)) as [string, string];
if (status === 'done') markComplete(id);
```

Right — named fields, validated at the boundary:

```ts
const Job = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  status: z.enum(['queued', 'running', 'done', 'failed']),
});
const job = Job.parse(await getJob(jobId)); // order-independent, unknown keys rejected
if (job.status === 'done') markComplete(job.id);
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced where data enters, not where it is discussed:

- **Schema validation at every boundary** (zod, JSON Schema, protobuf/Avro): parse, do not hand-check; reject unknown keys; fail fast at entry.
- **Consumer-driven contract tests** (Pact): producer CI runs against real consumer expectations, catching drift before deploy.
- **OpenAPI spec as the source of truth in CI**: the spec exists, matches the implementation via round-trip tests, and every PR's diff is classified.
- **Schema registry with compatibility checks** for events: producers cannot merge a breaking shape change.
- **Shared contract packages**, versioned and published — one definition, not N copies.

## Real-world case

A consumer built its mapping on the field order of a producer's JSON response — never documented, just observed. The producer later fixed what it considered a harmless sort bug, changing element order. The consumer's positional logic then mapped IDs to the wrong records, and the mismatch flowed into downstream reports for days before a reconciliation flagged it; nobody connected the "harmless" sort fix to the corrupted mapping. A named-field schema would have reduced a multi-day silent corruption to a failing contract test in CI. (ilustratif — composite of a common failure mode; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Validation cost vs. throughput**: parsing every inbound message costs CPU at high volume; validate at boundaries and pass typed, trusted data inward — not repeated checks in-process.
- **Strictness vs. tolerance**: the Robustness Principle argues for accepting imperfect input; this principle argues for rejecting the undefined. Resolution: tolerance is a documented, logged exception inside the contract — never folklore.
- **Schema ceremony vs. velocity**: writing contracts first feels slow; it is still cheaper than the 3 a.m. version, and consumer-driven tests turn it into a safety net rather than paperwork.

## Related principles

- [Versioned Contracts](/docs/principles/api/versioned-contracts) — how a declared contract evolves safely.
- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — why the undeclared parts still behave like a contract.
- [Input Validation](/docs/principles/security/input-validation) — the hostile-boundary, security-grade version.
- [Robustness Principle](/docs/principles/api/postel-robustness) — bounded tolerance inside a declared contract.
- [Expand-Contract](/docs/principles/data/expand-contract) — the procedure for changing schemas consumers already read.
- [Fail-Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — reject loudly at the boundary instead of corrupting quietly inside.

## References

- Google SRE Book — reliability as a boundary and API problem: https://sre.google/sre-book/ (verified URL).
- Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* — data models and evolution as contract design (verification: perlu — confirm chapter before citing precisely).

## Versioned Contracts
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/api/versioned-contracts
- Category: api · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Public contracts change only through versions with deprecation windows — never mutate the meaning of an existing one.
> Change any published contract only through a new version, and keep the old one working through an announced deprecation window. Never alter the meaning of an existing version — not a field's type, not an error code, not a default. Before removing anything, measure who still uses it, and sunset on evidence, not on hope.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Once a contract is public, its meaning is frozen: changes ship as new versions (semver majors for libraries, API versions for services, expand-contract steps for databases), while the old version is deprecated, monitored, and eventually removed on a published schedule. Silently mutating semantics under the same version number is the cardinal sin — it breaks consumers who did everything right. Versioning is how you keep the freedom to change without claiming the right to surprise.

## When to use

- Public API surfaces and shared libraries with consumers you do not control.
- Team-facing internal APIs where consumers deploy independently.
- Database schema changes read by other services — paired with expand-contract.
- Any removal, rename, type change, or behavioral change to something already shipped.

## When NOT to use

- Pre-1.0 experimentation where consumers knowingly accept churn — that is semver's own 0.x convention.
- Single-consumer internal tooling deployed in lockstep with its caller.
- Security emergencies: still versioned, but the window collapses to "announce loudly, fix now" — weigh the harm against the breakage instead of waiting out a calendar.

## Anti-pattern

- A response field silently changes type from string to number inside the same version.
- A "minor" release renames a column or tightens validation that used to pass.
- Deprecation by exception — it throws now, so callers "know".
- Removing a field or package because "nobody should be using that" — Hyrum's Law guarantees somebody is.
- Deprecating without usage metrics: the sunset date is a guess, and the guess is somebody's outage.

## Code example

Wrong — same version, new meaning:

```ts
// GET /v1/plans — price used to be "19.99" (decimal string); now 1999 (cents)
app.get('/v1/plans', (req, res) => {
  res.json(plans.map(p => ({ ...p, price: p.priceCents }))); // silent type flip
});
```

Right — additive change, old meaning carried through a deprecation window:

```ts
app.get('/v1/plans', (req, res) => {
  res.json(plans.map(p => ({
    ...p,
    price: (p.priceCents / 100).toFixed(2), // v1 meaning preserved — unchanged
    price_cents: p.priceCents,              // additive; old field gets a deprecation header
  })));
});
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced by CI gates and counters, not by release notes:

- **Semver linters and API diff gates**: semantic-release or API diff tools fail the build when a breaking shape change ships without a version bump.
- **OpenAPI diff in CI**: every PR's contract delta is classified (breaking / additive / compatible), and breaking changes require a new version marker.
- **Deprecation headers and metrics**: announce via response headers, track per-field and per-endpoint usage, and gate removal on the measured consumer count reaching zero.
- **Consumer-driven contract tests** (Pact): old consumers keep passing until the sunset actually executes.
- **Database**: expand-contract migrations — add new, dual-write, migrate readers, and only then remove old.

## Real-world case

An API team changed one response field's type from decimal string to number — a "cleanup", unversioned, in a routine release. Because JSON happily carries both, nothing failed loudly: integrators with strict parsers broke in their own runtimes, while others silently mis-rounded prices. One customer found it in billing reconciliation weeks later, and the incident review had no deprecation metrics to even measure who was affected. A version bump with a window would have reduced, not prevented, the breakage — integrators still had to change code, but on a schedule they chose. The removal-without-warning cousin is left-pad 2016: a package vanished with no version, no window, and thousands of builds broke — https://www.theregister.com/2016/03/23/npm_left_pad_chaos/ (verified URL). (ilustratif for the type-flip scenario; verification: perlu)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Compatibility vs. velocity**: versioning every change is ceremony; the compromise is additive-by-default — backward-compatible additions need no new major, only meaning changes do.
- **Versioned vs. leaked behavior**: Hyrum's Law guarantees even versioned surfaces leak observable details (timing, pagination order); version what you can, monitor what you cannot.
- **Windows vs. urgency**: long deprecation windows protect slow consumers but double the surface you maintain; size the window on usage metrics, not politeness.

## Related principles

- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — why the old version's behavior is depended on even where undocumented.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — you cannot version what was never declared.
- [Expand-Contract](/docs/principles/data/expand-contract) — the database-schema version of this principle.
- [Soft-Delete](/docs/principles/data/soft-delete) — deprecation is soft-delete for contracts: remove only with evidence.
- [Robustness Principle](/docs/principles/api/postel-robustness) — retiring a tolerated deviation must itself go through a version.
- [Supply-Chain Vetting](/docs/principles/security/supply-chain-vetting) — pin and review what you depend on before someone else's version change becomes your outage.

## References

- Semantic Versioning 2.0.0: https://semver.org (verified URL).
- The Register, npm left-pad aftermath, March 2016: https://www.theregister.com/2016/03/23/npm_left_pad_chaos/ (verified URL).

---

## Hyrum's Law
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law
- Category: api · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: With enough users, every observable behavior of your system will be depended on by somebody — including the ones you never promised.
> Treat everything a consumer can observe — field order, error text, timing, package existence — as part of your contract. Before changing any observable behavior, find out who depends on it, communicate through a version and a deprecation window, and measure usage until the last consumer has migrated. Never dismiss a break with "it was undocumented".

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

When the number of consumers of an interface is large enough, every observable behavior will be depended on by somebody, regardless of what the contract promises. The real interface is what consumers actually use: response shapes, error messages, rate-limit timing, the presence of a field nobody documented. Changing such behavior — even fixing it — is a breaking change and must be priced, communicated, and versioned as one.

## When to use

- Any public or shared API, library, or event stream with consumers you do not control.
- Evaluating "harmless" bug fixes that alter observable output.
- Planning deprecations, removals, or major version bumps.
- Reviewing database or storage shapes that other teams read directly.

## When NOT to use

- As a veto over security or correctness fixes — when the behavior is harmful, ship the fix and manage the window, loudly.
- Internal code with a single consumer you also own, deployed in lockstep.
- Pre-launch code with no real consumers yet — the law has no subjects until someone depends on the behavior.

## Anti-pattern

- "It's not in the docs, so we can change it" — with a large consumer base, that is never true.
- Consumers parsing error message strings, or timing requests to infer internal state — and producers obliging forever.
- Returning ORM rows straight from an endpoint: every internal column becomes someone's contract.
- Removing a dependency or field because "nobody uses it" — without usage metrics to prove it.

## Code example

Wrong — the storage shape leaks; the ORM's columns become the contract:

```ts
app.get('/users/:id', async (req, res) => {
  const row = await db.users.find({ id: req.params.id });
  res.json(row); // createdAt, internal flags, future columns: all observed, all depended on
});
```

Right — the contract is chosen, typed, and validated:

```ts
const UserDTO = z.object({ id: z.string(), name: z.string() }).strict();
app.get('/users/:id', async (req, res) => {
  const row = await db.users.find({ id: req.params.id });
  res.json(UserDTO.parse({ id: row.id, name: row.display_name })); // pick, don't leak
});
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is enforced by machinery, not by careful consumers:

- **Consumer-driven contract tests** (Pact) in CI on both producer and consumer sides: the verified contract is what consumers actually use, not what the docs claim.
- **Explicit DTOs and serializers**: internal shapes never cross the boundary unfiltered.
- **API diff gates**: OpenAPI diffing in CI classifies changes and blocks breaking ones that lack a version bump.
- **Deprecation metrics**: per-field and per-endpoint usage tracking; removal is allowed only when the counter reaches zero — or an explicit, communicated sunset date passes.

## Real-world case

In March 2016, a developer unpublished his own packages from npm after a naming dispute; among them was left-pad, a tiny string-padding utility. Fresh installs and CI pipelines across the JavaScript ecosystem failed — thousands of dependent builds, including major frameworks' toolchains. Nobody ever contracted for the continued existence of that package; the ecosystem's build pipelines depended on it all the same. Exact-version pinning and registry-level removal policies would have reduced the blast radius, not prevented it — the dependency formed with or without a contract. Coverage: https://www.theregister.com/2016/03/23/npm_left_pad_chaos/ (verified URL).

## Tension and trade-off

- **Stability vs. progress**: this law prices every fix; the honest response is versioned change with a deprecation window, not freezing (see Versioned Contracts).
- **Hyrum vs. minimal surfaces**: the fewer observable details you expose — DTOs over raw rows, opaque IDs over sequential ones — the less there is to depend on. Design as if everything visible will become permanent.
- **Empathy vs. entitlement**: some dependencies are consumer abuse (parsing error strings); you may still break them, but deliberately, with notice and a migration path — not out of surprise.

## Related principles

- [Versioned Contracts](/docs/principles/api/versioned-contracts) — the sanctioned way to change what consumers depend on.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — shrink the implicit surface by declaring the explicit one.
- [Robustness Principle](/docs/principles/api/postel-robustness) — liberal acceptance multiplies the observable behaviors consumers attach to.
- [Supply-Chain Vetting](/docs/principles/security/supply-chain-vetting) — left-pad is also a supply-chain story: know what you transitively depend on.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — the scope of what a break can take down.
- [Expand-Contract](/docs/principles/data/expand-contract) — the Hyrum-aware procedure for schema changes.

## References

- Hyrum's Law: https://www.hyrumslaw.com (verified URL).
- The Register, npm left-pad aftermath, March 2016: https://www.theregister.com/2016/03/23/npm_left_pad_chaos/ (verified URL).
