# Category: security

## Least Authority
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/security/least-authority
- Category: security · Severity: critical · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Grant only the authority a task actually needs — a cleanup script with full write access turns a small bug into a deleted database.
> Always scope credentials, permissions, and runtime authority to the minimum needed for the specific task at hand. Never run scripts, agents, or services with admin/root/write-everything access when a narrower role exists. If a task appears to require broad authority, stop and ask a human before proceeding.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: critical.**

## Definition

Every program, script, agent, and person should operate with the smallest set of permissions sufficient for the task — and no more. Authority here means credentials, IAM roles, database users, file permissions, API scopes, and runtime capabilities. If the task only needs to read, the credential must only be able to read.

## When to use

- Operational scripts (cleanup, backfill, migration, export) — the default context for this principle.
- CI/CD pipelines and deploy jobs.
- Long-running services and AI agents acting on external systems.
- Any human account that also has a day-to-day non-admin role.

## When NOT to use

- One-time, time-boxed incident response where a human operator deliberately escalates for firefighting — and revokes afterwards.
- Local development sandboxes with no access to shared or production state.
- Seeding a brand-new, empty environment that is explicitly declared disposable.

## Anti-pattern

- A cleanup script connects with the admin account "because it was already in the env file".
- An agent gets the same AWS keys as the lead developer.
- A cron job runs as root to delete rows in one table.
- A read-only report tool holding a read-write connection string "just in case".

## Code example

Wrong — broad authority, destructive blast radius:

```bash
# Uses DATABASE_URL that belongs to the migration tool: full DDL + delete rights
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "DELETE FROM audit_events WHERE created_at < now() - interval '30 days';"
```

Right — scoped authority, minimum rights:

```bash
# Dedicated role with only what this job needs (SELECT is not even required)
psql "postgresql://cleanup_app:${CLEANUP_PASSWORD}@db/crm?options=--role=audit_purger" \
  -c "CALL purge_audit_events_older_than(interval '30 days');"
```

```sql
-- The DBA creates the narrow role once; the script inherits it
CREATE ROLE audit_purger NOLOGIN;
GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION purge_audit_events_older_than(interval) TO audit_purger;
GRANT audit_purger TO cleanup_app;
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is not enforced by prompts. Enforce it with real controls:

- **Scoped credentials**: separate read-only / write-limited database users and IAM roles per job; the admin secret lives in a vault, never in the job's environment.
- **Static analysis + policy checks in CI**: reject PRs that reference admin roles for scheduled jobs (e.g. custom lint, cloud policy engines).
- **Runtime policy**: database permissions, IAM boundaries, and Kubernetes RBAC that make "accidentally too much" impossible even if the script is wrong.
- **Auditing**: every grant and every use of a privileged role is logged and reviewed.

## Real-world case

In January 2017, a GitLab operator, exhausted after a long day of replication failures, deleted the wrong directory on the primary database server — believing it held a secondary's data. The directory held the primary's live data. Because the tooling and credentials allowed that action from where he was working, hundreds of gigabytes of data (issues, merge requests, users) were gone; six hours of writes were permanently lost after restoring from backups that were slower and less complete than expected. Postmortem: https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2017/02/01/gitlab-dotcom-database-incident/ — narrower authority at that shell, and human-confirmation before an irreversible delete, would have contained the mistake. (verification: perlu for link details — read the postmortem before citing further.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Velocity vs. safety**: broad credentials are faster to wire up and annoying to split. The cost of least authority is paid in setup, not in incidents — pay it once per environment.
- **Least Authority vs. automation ambition**: an agent that can "do anything" demos better. Scope authority to the task graph you actually have, and extend deliberately when new needs are proven, not preemptively.
- **Weigh against Least Astonishment**: do not split authority so finely that operators cannot predict which credential does what — few, clearly-scoped roles beat many confusing ones.

## Related principles

- [Fail-Safe Defaults](/docs/principles/security/fail-safe-defaults) — deny by default, grant explicitly; the complement of least authority.
- [Defense in Depth](/docs/principles/security/defense-in-depth) — layered controls when authority scoping cannot be perfect.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — limit the maximum damage of any single action.
- [Tested Backups](/docs/principles/data/tested-backups) — the last line of defense when everything else failed.

## References

- Saltzer & Schroeder, *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems*, Proceedings of the IEEE, 1975 — origin of "least privilege" (verification: perlu — find a stable public copy before linking).
- NIST SP 800-207, *Zero Trust Architecture* — modern framing of per-task authority (verification: perlu).

---

## Supply Chain Vetting
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/security/supply-chain-vetting
- Category: security · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Every dependency is a stranger with commit access to your production — pin, audit, and review before adopting.
> Treat every dependency as code that will run with your permissions in production. Never install a package you have not checked: maintainer history, release activity, install scripts, transitive footprint. Always pin exact versions and commit lock files; never resolve version ranges automatically. If a dependency suddenly changes maintainers or behavior, stop and investigate before upgrading.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Third-party code executes with your authority, inside your trust boundary, from the moment you install it. Supply chain vetting means each dependency is chosen deliberately — maintained, understood, minimal — and then held fixed by lock files and digests so what you audited is what you run. The question is never "is this package useful" but "is this package, its maintainer situation, and everything it pulls in, worth executing with my credentials".

## When to use

- Adding any new dependency, direct or transitive, to a production codebase.
- CI and build images — where strangers' code runs with your secrets present.
- Base images, actions, plugins, and CLIs installed into pipelines.
- Scheduled maintenance: reviewing the dependency list you already have.

## When NOT to use

- Time-boxed prototypes that never touch production state or credentials — deleted or vetted before promotion.
- When vendoring a tiny, frozen utility (read it, audit it, copy it, pin it) is cheaper than the ongoing trust relationship of depending on it.
- First-party internal packages where vetting is replaced by ownership — your own team is the maintainer being trusted.

## Anti-pattern

- Installing the first package whose name matches the error message.
- Version ranges in a manifest, so the next clean build silently resolves different code than the last one.
- Piping install scripts from a project README straight into CI.
- A lock file with hundreds of packages nobody chose and nobody can name.
- Using download counts and stars as a proxy for maintenance health and maintainer continuity.

## Code example

Wrong — floating range, blind install:

```bash
npm install some-utils@^1.0.0       # a range, not a pin
# Later builds resolve whatever 1.x currently is: unreviewed, possibly
# published by someone new. CI is now an amusement ride, not a pipeline.
```

Right — pin, lock, audit:

```bash
# Pin the exact version; the lock file is the real dependency contract
npm install --save-exact some-utils@1.3.0
npm ci                      # installs ONLY what the lock file records

# Fail the build on known vulnerabilities in the direct dependency set
npm audit --omit=dev        # a CI gate, not a suggestion
```

## Technical enforcement

Vetting must be a pipeline stage, not a code-review hero moment:

- **Lock files as the contract**: CI installs with frozen lock files — fresh resolution is a build failure, not a habit.
- **Lock file diffs in review**: every dependency change appears in the pull request as an explicit, human-readable record of what changed and why.
- **Vulnerability gates**: audit steps that fail the pipeline on known CVEs in the direct dependency set.
- **Registry policies**: allowlists or internal proxies for builds; no live installs from public registries inside production images.
- **Digest pinning for images and actions**: reference digests, not tags — tags are mutable, digests are not.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: lock files and digests prevent silent code changes between builds; audits and diffs detect risk you already accepted — both halves, always.

## Real-world case

Two npm incidents show both halves of the risk. In March 2016, the package left-pad — eleven lines of code — was unpublished from npm, and builds across the ecosystem broke within hours: thousands of projects depended on availability and naming that nobody had promised them. https://www.theregister.com/2016/03/23/npm_left_pad_chaos/ In November 2018, event-stream showed the other half: a long-time maintainer handed the package to a stranger, the new maintainer added a targeted malicious dependency that stole wallet credentials from a specific product's users, and the legitimate-looking version passed unremarked through thousands of installs. https://github.com/dominictarr/event-stream/issues/116 Pinning would not have prevented either event, but it would have reduced the damage: the unpublish becomes a build error you chose to freeze, and the malicious version requires a deliberate, reviewed upgrade instead of arriving on the next clean build.

## Tension and trade-off

- **Vetting vs. KISS**: every gate slows down the "just install it" loop that makes package managers glorious — set the bar by the dependency's blast radius, not by uniform ceremony.
- **Pinning vs. staying patched**: a frozen dependency receives no fixes by itself; pair pinning with a scheduled, reviewed upgrade cadence, and make a skipped security upgrade fail loudly in CI rather than silently in production.
- **Minimizing dependencies vs. DRY tension**: DRY pushes toward extracting and sharing code, but every shared package is a maintainer relationship you inherit — sharing has a supply-chain cost.

## Related principles

- [Least Authority](/docs/principles/security/least-authority) — CI credentials scoped so a compromised dependency cannot sign your releases.
- [Secrets Hygiene](/docs/principles/security/secrets-hygiene) — the token a compromised package is really after.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — what an exploded dependency can actually reach.
- [Fail Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — lock file drift and audit findings must be loud.
- [DRY Tension](/docs/principles/design/dry-tension) — when sharing code stops being free.

## References

- Saltzer & Schroeder, *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems*, Proceedings of the IEEE, 1975 — least common mechanism: shared components are shared risk.
- semver.org — what version numbers promise, and what they do not: https://semver.org

---

## Complete Mediation
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/security/complete-mediation
- Category: security · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Authorize every access through every path — a cached permission or a forgotten side door is still a door.
> Authorize every access on every path — every request, every background job, every side door. Never trust a permission decided earlier: not at login, not at session start, not because the object was reachable in a previous request. If you find a path that skips the check, treat it as a vulnerability and report it.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Every access to every protected object must pass through an authorization check — not at login, not at page load, but at the moment of access, on the path that performs it. Cached authority decisions are snapshots of the past: roles change, ownership changes, tokens get revoked, and the check skipped "because we already checked" is skipped at exactly the wrong time. Saltzer and Schroeder named this complete mediation, and it is the principle most often violated by convenience: decorators on some endpoints, an assumed check "further up", a worker that reads the same data without the gate.

## When to use

- APIs with per-object access rules: document, project, and workspace scoped resources.
- Long-lived sessions and tokens: web apps, mobile apps, agents.
- Async and background paths: workers, schedulers, webhooks — the doors people forget.
- Any system where roles, memberships, or ownership can change while sessions are alive.

## When NOT to use

- Fully public resources where authorization is a no-op — an empty check is noise; mark the route explicitly public instead.
- Immutable, non-sensitive metadata that cannot change ownership — document the assumption, revisit it when the object model changes.
- Short-lived caches backed by real invalidation on revocation — that is mediation with engineering, not an exception; keep it only as long as the invalidation actually works.

## Anti-pattern

- "Is logged in" treated as an authorization model — authentication reused as permission.
- The admin check done in the menu rendering code; the endpoint itself assumes only admins know the URL.
- A permission decision cached at session start and never revisited.
- A new admin endpoint added "temporarily" without the middleware, because it was an internal demo.
- A worker processing jobs by reading documents straight from the database, "because the API already checked when the job was created".

## Code example

Wrong — check once, trust forever:

```python
# Role resolved ONCE at login and stored in the session
@app.post("/login")
def login(user):
    session["role"] = db.get_role(user.id)      # snapshot of the past

@app.delete("/documents/{doc_id}")
def delete_document(doc_id):
    if session["role"] != "admin":              # hours stale, checked anyway
        abort(403)
    db.delete(doc_id)                           # authority from this morning
```

Right — check at the moment of access, on the path that performs it:

```python
# Authority resolved per access, against the current role and THIS object
@app.delete("/documents/{doc_id}")
@require_permission("document:delete", doc_id)  # fresh role + this doc
def delete_document(doc_id):
    db.delete(doc_id)

# The decorator resolves the CURRENT role (cached only with invalidation
# on revocation) and ownership of THIS document — every request, every path.
```

## Technical enforcement

Mediation must be structural so new code cannot opt out:

- **A single authorization point**: framework-level guards that every route must declare — a route without an explicit policy fails startup, deny by default at the routing layer.
- **Object-level, not just route-level checks**: policies evaluated against the specific resource, kept in one place by ABAC/RBAC libraries or a policy engine.
- **Revocation that propagates**: role changes and token revocations invalidate or expire cached decisions; short session lifetimes and token introspection bound staleness by design, not by hope.
- **Coverage tests and route inventory audits**: a test that fails when any route or worker touches a protected model without passing the policy point.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: guards and startup failures prevent unmediated paths from shipping; audits and coverage tests detect the ones that slipped — mediation decays quietly, so keep the detection half funded.

## Real-world case

Scenario (ilustratif): an application resolves the user's role once, at session start, and caches it for the session's lifetime. The user's admin role is revoked mid-session — an offboarding, a security response — but every request still carries yesterday's answer: for hours, until the session expires, the ex-admin can create, read, and delete with authority that was already withdrawn. There is no single bug to fix; the design asked "is this user an admin" at the wrong time and trusted the answer forever. Mediating every access — resolving authority at the moment of use, with revocation invalidating cached decisions — would have reduced the exposure from hours of full access to seconds. (Ilustratif; verification: perlu — no public postmortem is cited here.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Per-access checks vs. latency**: every access through the policy point costs a lookup; caches are the honest compromise — but a stale cache either over-grants, violating least authority, or under-grants, locking out real users against least astonishment. Set the staleness budget explicitly and wire revocation to invalidation.
- **Fail-closed mediation vs. graceful degradation**: when the policy store is unreachable, failing closed protects the data but darkens the product, while failing open opens the doors — decide per path, and decide before the outage.
- **One mediation point vs. single responsibility**: singular enforcement is the point, but one policy module owned by everyone owns nothing — distribute the policy definitions, keep the enforcement point singular.

## Related principles

- [Least Authority](/docs/principles/security/least-authority) — what the answer of each check should be.
- [Fail-Safe Defaults](/docs/principles/security/fail-safe-defaults) — what mediation does when the checker itself fails.
- [Input Validation](/docs/principles/security/input-validation) — the twin gate at the boundary: validate the data, mediate the authority.
- [Single Responsibility](/docs/principles/architecture/single-responsibility) — keep the policy point singular without making it a dumping ground.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — permission requirements declared per route, not implied.

## References

- Saltzer & Schroeder, *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems*, Proceedings of the IEEE, 1975 — complete mediation is one of the original design principles.
- NIST SP 800-207, *Zero Trust Architecture*, 2020 — continuous, per-request evaluation instead of one-time perimeter trust: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-207.pdf

---

## Input Validation
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/security/input-validation
- Category: security · Severity: critical · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Validate every input at the trust boundary before it touches state — reject early, completely, and unambiguously.
> Validate every input at the trust boundary — request bodies, headers, query strings, file contents, queue messages, model inputs — before it reaches storage, commands, or business logic. Never trust a caller, a partner service, or your own frontend to have already validated. If you cannot state precisely what valid looks like, stop and ask a human before writing the handler.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: critical.**

## Definition

Every place data crosses from a less-trusted context into a more-trusted one is a trust boundary, and everything crossing it must be checked for type, shape, size, range, and encoding before it touches state. Validation is the doorman, not the cleanup crew: malformed input is rejected at the door, not repaired downstream where its meaning is unknown. The same goes for lengths and bounds — the check belongs at the boundary, not "eventually".

## When to use

- API endpoints and webhooks — the canonical boundary.
- Database layers that accept writes from more than one producer.
- Queue and stream consumers: messages often outlive the code that produced them.
- Imports, uploads, and ML pipelines: training data, files, third-party feeds.
- Anything shell commands, queries, or file paths are built from.

## When NOT to use

- Inside a single module whose inputs were already validated at its public boundary — re-validating every internal call is noise.
- Telemetry and logging pipelines that must never crash: capture what parses, count the rest as dropped.
- Stores whose contract is to hold bytes opaquely — validation belongs to whoever interprets the blob later.

## Anti-pattern

- Validating only the fields the current UI sends; a new field arrives with no check.
- Sanitizing by string replacement — strip quotes, escape dashes — instead of parsing into a known-good structure.
- Trusting an internal service "because it is ours"; the boundary still exists.
- Enforcing lengths in the frontend and assuming only the frontend calls the API.
- Silently repairing malformed input: coercing, trimming, guessing — then continuing with a value nobody sent.

## Code example

Wrong — string-splicing a query from unvalidated input:

```python
# No boundary check: type, shape, and length are all assumptions
def find_orders(request):
    user_id = request.args.get("user_id")
    status = request.args.get("status", "open")
    sql = f"SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = {user_id} AND status = '{status}'"
    return db.execute(sql)     # one crafted user_id reads the whole table
```

Right — parse, validate, reject at the boundary:

```python
def find_orders(request):
    try:
        user_id = parse_uuid(request.args["user_id"])       # exact type
        status = request.args.get("status", "open")
        if status not in {"open", "paid", "shipped"}:       # closed allowlist
            raise ValueError("bad status")
    except (KeyError, ValueError) as e:
        return reject(400, str(e))     # rejected at the door, state untouched
    return db.query(Order).filter_by(user_id=user_id, status=status).all()
```

## Technical enforcement

Validation must be structural, not aspirational:

- **Schema-first APIs**: typed request schemas that reject unknown or malformed fields before handler code runs — validation as plumbing, not discipline.
- **Parameterized access paths only**: parameterized queries, prepared statements, safe path-join helpers; CI bans string-built SQL and shell commands.
- **Limits at the gateway**: request size caps, field length caps, and timeouts before expensive parsing begins.
- **Fuzzing in CI**: malformed inputs generated against every endpoint; crashes and leaks fail the build.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: schemas and parameterization prevent malformed data from ever reaching logic; fuzzing and logs detect the gaps after attempts — run both, never assume the first is complete.

## Real-world case

Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160), disclosed in April 2014, was a missing bounds check exactly at a trust boundary: OpenSSL's TLS heartbeat extension took a claimed payload length from the peer and echoed back that many bytes without verifying the buffer actually held them. A crafted message claiming a large payload let attackers read server memory — session tokens, passwords, and in the worst case private keys — with no trace in the logs. The input was trusted precisely where it should have been measured. Rigorous boundary validation would not have prevented every future OpenSSL bug, but it would have reduced this one from "read arbitrary process memory remotely" to "reject a malformed heartbeat". Details: https://heartbleed.com/

## Tension and trade-off

- **Validation vs. Postel's robustness**: being liberal in what you accept buys interoperability and hides caller bugs; at a security boundary, strictness wins — be liberal only where you can afford to guess.
- **Tightening validation vs. versioned contracts**: stricter rules reject clients the old contract allowed — tighten through a new version, not by ambushing existing ones.
- **Early rejection vs. graceful degradation**: rejecting malformed input fast protects state, but a flood of bad traffic can become a user-visible storm — pair rejection with rate limiting and clear errors.

## Related principles

- [Fail-Safe Defaults](/docs/principles/security/fail-safe-defaults) — what happens with input you did not plan for.
- [Defense in Depth](/docs/principles/security/defense-in-depth) — validation is the outer wall, not the only one.
- [Complete Mediation](/docs/principles/security/complete-mediation) — the access-control twin: validate the data and the authority, every time.
- [Postel's Robustness](/docs/principles/api/postel-robustness) — the tension, stated honestly.
- [Versioned Contracts](/docs/principles/api/versioned-contracts) — how to tighten validation without ambushing clients.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — validation rules belong in the contract, not in tribal memory.

## References

- Hunt & Thomas, *The Pragmatic Programmer*, 1999 — on crashing early rather than working with data you cannot trust.
- RFC 1122, *Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers*, 1989 — the robustness principle and what it costs at trust boundaries: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122

---

## Defense in Depth
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/security/defense-in-depth
- Category: security · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: No single control is perfect — layer independent controls so one failure never becomes a breach.
> Never rely on a single control to stop a security failure. When you design a boundary, assume the control in front of it will eventually fail — a bug, a misconfiguration, an expired certificate — and place an independent layer behind it. If removing one layer would leave the system unprotected, stop and redesign the boundary.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Every control fails eventually: code has bugs, configurations drift, certificates expire, people get tired. Defense in depth arranges multiple, independent controls so a single failure is contained by the next layer instead of becoming the incident. Independence is the load-bearing word — three copies of the same check share one failure mode and are one control wearing a costume.

## When to use

- Security-critical paths: authentication, authorization, payments, key handling.
- Boundaries facing untrusted input: public APIs, file uploads, network edges.
- Infrastructure where misconfiguration is a realistic failure mode — it usually is.
- Any system whose single security failure would also be a business-ending event.

## When NOT to use

- Prototypes with no real data, where one honest layer plus fast iteration beats three aspirational layers nobody maintains.
- "Depth" made of copies: the same check duplicated in different places shares its failure mode — consolidate and build a genuinely different control instead.
- Latency-critical paths guarding low-value assets, where every extra hop costs more than the thing it protects.

## Anti-pattern

- "The WAF blocks it, so the app does not need to validate input."
- A private network treated as the only boundary: anything that gets inside owns everything.
- Secrets protected by file permissions alone, with no vault and no rotation behind them.
- Monitoring that would tell you about a breach, running on the same infrastructure the breach takes down.
- One penetration test passed years ago, declared secure forever.

## Code example

Wrong — one layer, total exposure when it fails:

```javascript
// The ONLY thing between the internet and account deletion is the network rule
app.post("/admin/delete-user", (req, res) => {
  // trusted because the load balancer only forwards internal traffic here
  deleteUser(req.body.userId);   // one misconfigured routing rule and prod is wide open
});
```

Right — independent layers behind the boundary:

```javascript
// Layer 1: network rule. Layer 2: app-level role check on every request.
app.post("/admin/delete-user", requireRole("admin"), (req, res) => {
  // Layer 3: audit trail of who deleted what. Layer 4: soft, recoverable delete.
  softDeleteUser(req.body.userId, { by: res.locals.user.id, reason: "admin-console" });
});
```

## Technical enforcement

Depth must live in the platform, not in individual memory:

- **Segmentation plus per-service authorization**: even a fully compromised pod still faces service-level auth checks and mutual TLS policies — not just the network perimeter.
- **A second authorization path**: policy engines or IAM conditions evaluated independently of application code, so an app bug does not decide access alone.
- **Off-host, append-only audit logs**: evidence that survives the very compromise it records.
- **Recoverable destruction**: soft deletes and tested backups so a defeated application layer is not the end of the story.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: segmentation and per-service auth stop movement after a breach; logs and alerts detect what already happened. You need both — detection is the layer that tells you the others failed.

## Real-world case

In February 2014, Apple's iOS and OS X releases were found to contain a duplicated "goto fail" line inside the certificate-validation function. The extra unconditional jump skipped the checks that verify a server's certificate chain, yet the function still returned success — TLS connections were accepted with any certificate. The one layer responsible for validation failed silently, and there was no second layer behind it: no independent pinning check, no validator that disagreed, no test exercising the failure path. Defense in depth would not have made the typo impossible — it would have reduced the exposure: an independent validation or pinning layer would have caught connections the broken function approved. Details: https://www.imperialviolet.org/2014/02/22/applebug.html

## Tension and trade-off

- **Depth vs. KISS**: every layer adds configuration surface, failure modes, and debugging pain; put depth on critical paths, not uniformly everywhere.
- **Depth vs. Observability-First**: layers that fail quietly turn debugging into archaeology — per-layer logging is part of the layer, not an optional extra.
- **Depth vs. Yagni**: speculative layers against hypothetical attacks cost real maintenance forever; scale the depth to what a breach would actually cost.

## Related principles

- [Fail-Safe Defaults](/docs/principles/security/fail-safe-defaults) — each layer should fail toward denial, not toward openness.
- [Least Authority](/docs/principles/security/least-authority) — bounds what any single compromised layer can reach.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — layers exist to shrink the reachable damage set.
- [Soft Delete](/docs/principles/data/soft-delete) — recoverable destruction as the last defensive layer.
- [Append-Only Logs](/docs/principles/data/append-only-logs) — evidence designed to survive the incident.

## References

- Saltzer & Schroeder, *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems*, Proceedings of the IEEE, 1975 — separation of privilege: requiring multiple conditions before granting access.
- NIST SP 800-207, *Zero Trust Architecture*, 2020 — layered, per-request defenses: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-207.pdf

---

## Fail-Safe Defaults
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/security/fail-safe-defaults
- Category: security · Severity: critical · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Deny by default and grant explicitly — permission must be earned per action, not assumed until revoked.
> Default every decision, flag, and permission to the denying or non-destructive state. Never let a destructive action run because a safety flag was forgotten or a check failed open. If a failure, timeout, or error leaves you uncertain whether something is allowed, deny and ask a human.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: critical.**

## Definition

When a system fails, is uncertain, or simply starts fresh, it must fall into a state that denies access and skips destructive action. Permission is a positive, explicit grant per action — never an assumption that persists until someone remembers to revoke it. This is Saltzer and Schroeder's fail-safe defaults: base access decisions on permission rather than exclusion, because the default situation is no permission at all.

## When to use

- Destructive operations: deletes, drops, force-pushes, purges, teardowns, bulk updates.
- API and service access control: authentication and authorization on every path.
- Scripts and automation run by tired humans, in the wrong window, on the wrong server.
- New features and flags: ship disabled, enable deliberately, per environment.

## When NOT to use

- Public, read-only content where denial would defeat the product's purpose — the anonymous grant is explicit and global, not a forgotten default.
- Liveness endpoints that must keep answering during partial failure so the orchestrator does not kill every instance at once — a deliberate, documented fail-open.
- Environments explicitly declared disposable, where denial protects nothing.

## Anti-pattern

- A cleanup CLI where the destructive run is the default and the dry-run flag must be remembered every time.
- An admin endpoint left accessible to any authenticated user because the role check was never written.
- Firewall rules written as "allow everything, then deny the bad ports".
- An auth-service timeout that lets the request through "to avoid blocking users".
- A flag whose old meaning is forgotten, so it now enables a code path nobody intended to run.

## Code example

Wrong — safety is opt-in, destruction is the default:

```bash
# The safe flag must be remembered on every single invocation.
./bin/purge-old-records --older-than 30d
# → connects to prod, deletes rows, no confirmation, no preview
# The one time the operator is tired, the safe behavior simply does not happen.
```

Right — destruction requires an explicit, per-run grant:

```python
# Deleting is opt-in; the default path can only ever print.
parser.add_argument("--older-than", required=True, help="age cutoff, e.g. 30d")
parser.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true",
                    help="actually delete; without this flag the script only prints")
args = parser.parse_args()
plan = select_records_older_than(args.older_than)
if not args.apply:
    print_plan(plan)        # fail-safe default: show, never touch
    sys.exit(0)
delete(plan)                # explicit grant, valid for this run only
```

## Technical enforcement

This principle is not enforced by willpower. Enforce it with real controls:

- **Deny-first middleware**: an authorization base policy applied to every route by construction; routes opt in to a permission, never out of the check.
- **Flags that start disabled**: feature-flag platforms where new flags default to off, and dead code paths require explicit per-environment enablement.
- **Fail-closed timeouts**: policy and auth lookups that time out deny the request; fail-open is an explicit, reviewed, documented exception.
- **Two-step destruction**: irreversible operations require a separate confirmation step or a second actor, enforced by the tooling, not by memory.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: default-deny middleware and disabled-by-default flags prevent the action even when the handler is buggy; audits of flags and grants only detect drift afterwards.

## Real-world case

On January 31, 2017, a GitLab operator, exhausted after hours of fighting replication failures, deleted a directory on the wrong server — the one holding the primary database's live data. The destructive command was available by default in his working context: nothing forced a dry run, a confirmation, or a second check before an irreversible delete. Roughly 300 GB of data was lost, and about six hours of database writes proved unrecoverable because the restores available were slower and less complete than expected. Fail-safe defaults would not have stopped the initial mistake, but they would have reduced a one-line command into a printed plan and a moment of embarrassment. Postmortem: https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2017/02/01/gitlab-dotcom-database-incident/

## Tension and trade-off

- **Fail-closed vs. graceful degradation**: when a dependency fails, denying everything converts its outage into yours — decide per path, before the incident, whether fail-closed is proportionate.
- **Deny by default vs. least astonishment**: operators who hit unpredictable denials learn reflexive force flags; grants must be easy to give, visible when given, and predictable to reason about.
- **Explicit grants vs. least authority**: per-action grants everywhere turn into ceremony; narrow each grant itself so renewing it is safe instead of annoying.

## Related principles

- [Least Authority](/docs/principles/security/least-authority) — the sibling rule: grants are narrow, and doubt means denial.
- [Secure by Default](/docs/principles/security/secure-by-default) — the same idea applied to shipped configuration.
- [Defense in Depth](/docs/principles/security/defense-in-depth) — default-deny is one layer, not the whole wall.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — containment for the day a denial fails or is bypassed.
- [Least Astonishment](/docs/principles/design/least-astonishment) — safe defaults that still make sense to the person hitting them.

## References

- Saltzer & Schroeder, *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems*, Proceedings of the IEEE, 1975 — fail-safe defaults is one of the original design principles.
- NIST SP 800-207, *Zero Trust Architecture*, 2020 — deny-by-default, per-request access decisions: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-207.pdf

---

## Secure by Default
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/security/secure-by-default
- Category: security · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: Ship the safe configuration as the default — security must be what you get, not what you remember to enable.
> Ship the safe configuration as the out-of-the-box default and require explicit opt-in for anything risky. Never enable a powerful feature — remote code execution, dynamic lookups, admin interfaces, debug endpoints — just because it is convenient for demos. If you cannot name the safe default for a feature, stop and ask a human before shipping it.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Whatever a library, framework, or service ships with enabled is what most installations will run forever. Secure by default means the fresh, unmodified install is the hardened one: encryption on, dangerous features off, debug interfaces unreachable, no default credentials. Anything that weakens posture requires an explicit, documented opt-in — defaults are a decision made on behalf of every user who will never read the documentation.

## When to use

- Libraries and frameworks distributed to people you will never meet or audit.
- Infrastructure templates and base images that create environments others inherit.
- Anything with a demo mode — demo configs have a habit of becoming production configs.
- Client SDKs whose default settings silently propagate into thousands of applications.

## When NOT to use

- One-off internal tools with a written threat model that explicitly accepts the risk.
- Teaching examples whose entire purpose is demonstrating the unsafe mechanism — clearly labeled, never internet-facing.
- When the safest default makes the thing unusable for most users: pick the strongest default that still works out of the box, then expose hardening switches for the rest.

## Anti-pattern

- A logging library that interprets and fetches URLs found inside log text.
- Admin dashboards bound to all interfaces with a default password.
- TLS verification disabled in the example code that everyone copies into production.
- Debug mode driven by an environment variable that production also sets.
- A "hardening guide" offered as a substitute for safe defaults — documentation is not a control.

## Code example

Wrong — the powerful feature is on unless you know to disable it:

```javascript
// Library default: any string passed to the logger can trigger a remote lookup.
const logger = createLogger({ app: "billing" });
// "messageLookup" defaults to true — convenient for demos, catastrophic in prod

logger.warn(`Payment failed for ${userInput}`);
// userInput came from a request field; the logger fetches what it finds there
```

Right — inert default, explicit opt-in with a scope:

```javascript
// Default is inert: log text is data, never executed or fetched.
const logger = createLogger({ app: "billing" });
logger.warn(`Payment failed for ${userInput}`);   // always just text

// The feature still exists — for people who ask for it by name:
// const logger = createLogger({
//   app: "billing",
//   messageLookup: { enabled: true, allowHosts: ["metrics.internal"] },
// });
```

## Technical enforcement

Defaults must be enforced where users cannot skip them:

- **Hardened base images and templates**: organization-wide images with debug off, no default credentials, current patches — teams inherit safety without acting.
- **Configuration linting in CI**: fail builds on known-insecure flags — TLS verification off, debug mode in deploy artifacts, wildcard network binds, default passwords.
- **Default-behavior tests**: a fresh-install test asserting the dangerous feature is off and the safe one is on — defaults are behavior, so test them like behavior.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: shipping safe defaults prevents misconfiguration for the silent majority who never configure anything; lint and audits detect the minority who opted out — keep both, they cover different people.

## Real-world case

In December 2021, Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) showed what an unsafe default costs at ecosystem scale. Apache Log4j 2 performed JNDI lookups on strings that passed through log messages, and the feature was enabled by default: any application that logged attacker-controlled input — usernames, headers, form fields — could be tricked into fetching and executing code from a remote server. The vulnerable configuration was not a mistake anyone made; it was the configuration everyone got. Teams worldwide spent weeks patching and inventorying exposure. Secure by default — lookups off unless explicitly enabled — would not have removed the parsing flaw itself, but would have reduced the exposed population from default installations everywhere to the much smaller set that deliberately turned the feature on. Advisory: https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/security.html

## Tension and trade-off

- **Secure defaults vs. least astonishment**: the safest default nobody can boot protects nothing — choose the strongest default that still works in the first five minutes.
- **Secure by default vs. Hyrum's Law**: the moment a default ships, someone depends on it; changing it later is a breaking change, so the unsafe convenience shipped today is a forced migration tomorrow.
- **Hardening vs. Yagni**: defaults armored against imaginary threat models become configuration mazes that users route around — harden for the threats the thing actually faces.

## Related principles

- [Fail-Safe Defaults](/docs/principles/security/fail-safe-defaults) — the access-control sibling: deny unless granted.
- [Defense in Depth](/docs/principles/security/defense-in-depth) — the default is the first layer, never the only one.
- [Least Astonishment](/docs/principles/design/least-astonishment) — the safe default should still make sense to whoever discovers it.
- [Explicit Contracts](/docs/principles/api/explicit-contracts) — opt-in switches with clear names and a documented blast radius.
- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — why changing a shipped default is a breaking change.

## References

- Saltzer & Schroeder, *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems*, Proceedings of the IEEE, 1975 — fail-safe defaults and psychological acceptability: defaults people can and will actually live with.
- NIST SP 800-207, *Zero Trust Architecture*, 2020 — secure defaults in enterprise architecture: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-207.pdf
- Hyrum's Law — the contract your defaults become: https://www.hyrumslaw.com

## Secrets Hygiene
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/security/secrets-hygiene
- Category: security · Severity: critical · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Secrets never live in code, logs, tickets, or history — one leak is permanent because git forgets nothing.
> Never write secrets into source files, configuration templates, commit messages, tickets, chat logs, or log output — not even temporary ones, not even in a private repository. Always read secrets from a vault or environment injection at runtime, and rotate immediately if a secret has touched a repo. If you find a secret in code, a paste, or a log, stop and report it to a human with its exact location.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: critical.**

## Definition

A secret is any credential whose disclosure breaks a security boundary: API keys, tokens, passwords, private keys, connection strings. Code and its history are broadcast media — a secret committed once is copied to every clone, CI log, and archive, and rewriting history does not un-leak it. Hygiene means secrets exist only in vaults and runtime injection, are scoped and rotated, and are treated as compromised the moment they touch anything someone else can read.

## When to use

- Writing any script, service, or CI job that authenticates to something.
- Committing configuration, infrastructure code, or container images — the classic leak sites.
- Debugging and logging: the moment you print request headers or environments.
- Handing an agent or automation credentials to work on your behalf.

## When NOT to use

- Public keys and other identifiers designed to be shared — mislabeling them as secrets creates alert fatigue, which hides the real ones.
- Test fixtures with structurally fake values that real systems reject — obviously invalid example keys are safe and useful.
- Encrypted secrets committed to a repo where the decryption key is injected by CI from a vault — an accepted practice in some teams, defensible only while the key truly never enters git.

## Anti-pattern

- A connection string with its password committed in an example env file — example files get real values pasted into them.
- A token pasted into a ticket comment "just for the sprint".
- The deploy key baked into the base image "because builds were failing".
- Logging full request headers and environments on every error path.
- Planning to revoke a leaked key "later this week" instead of now.
- Treating a private repo as a safe place: private repos get cloned, mirrored, and remembered by ex-employees.

## Code example

Wrong — the secret lives in the repo:

```bash
# The .env file was committed "temporarily" during a deploy fire:
#   DATABASE_URL=postgres://svc:realpassword@prod-db.internal:5432/billing
# One push later: every clone, CI log, and mirror of the repo holds it forever.
git rm .env && git commit -m "remove env"   # pointless — history still has it
```

Right — the repo references names; the runtime provides values:

```bash
# Repo contains only the reference; vault or CI injects the real value.
./deploy.sh                      # reads DATABASE_URL from the environment

# Defense in depth around the secret:
# - pre-commit secrets scanner: commit fails BEFORE history exists
# - vault issues short-lived DB credentials per deploy, not per quarter
# - if a leak is suspected: rotate FIRST, then investigate how it leaked
```

## Technical enforcement

Hygiene survives only as tooling:

- **Pre-commit and server-side secret scanning** on every push — including on history rewrites, which are themselves a red flag worth alerting on.
- **Vault plus short-lived credentials**: secrets issued per job per run (OIDC federation to cloud roles instead of long-lived keys), so a leaked token ages out in minutes.
- **CI masking and scoping**: secrets masked in logs and never exposed to pull requests from forks.
- **A rehearsed rotation runbook**: revoking and rotating one credential class end to end, practiced before it is needed.
- **What prevents vs. detects**: per-run federated credentials prevent leaks from mattering — the leaked thing expires before anyone uses it; scanners detect the leak after the fact. Detection tells you prevention was imperfect; do not ship the first without planning the second.

## Real-world case

Scenario (ilustratif): an engineer commits a working access token into a repository — inside a code sample, a config file, or a late-night fix — and automated scrapers find it within minutes to days. Because git history is effectively append-only, deleting the file leaves the token in every clone and archive that already exists; the only real remediation is revocation and rotation, under time pressure, with the attacker already holding a valid credential. A similar real-world event — a stolen npm token used in 2018 to publish malicious versions of an official package — should be verified against primary sources before citing further (verification: perlu). The lesson holds either way: treat any secret that has touched a repo as compromised, and make rotation so routine that it is boring. No URL is cited because this case is illustrative, not a specific verified incident.

## Tension and trade-off

- **Hygiene vs. KISS**: vault wiring, scopes, and rotation add real setup complexity; the boring minimal version — environment injection from a vault — beats the elaborate one nobody maintains.
- **Secrets vs. Observability-First**: debugging wants the exact failing credential and header values; mask by default and unmask only through a controlled, audited path.
- **Aggressive rotation vs. graceful degradation**: credentials that expire under a running service can take it down mid-flight; rotation needs overlap windows or live reload, and a failed rotation should fail loudly, not silently.

## Related principles

- [Least Authority](/docs/principles/security/least-authority) — a leaked scoped, short-lived credential is a papercut, not an amputation.
- [Secure by Default](/docs/principles/security/secure-by-default) — tools that demand secrets only at runtime, never in files.
- [Supply Chain Vetting](/docs/principles/security/supply-chain-vetting) — leaked CI tokens are exactly what malicious package publishes are made of.
- [Fail-Safe Defaults](/docs/principles/security/fail-safe-defaults) — when a secret is missing, fail closed instead of falling back to the committed one.
- [Observability First](/docs/principles/reliability/observability-first) — logs rich enough to debug, blind enough to keep.
- [Append-Only Logs](/docs/principles/data/append-only-logs) — why history never forgets, and why rotation is the only real fix.

## References

- Saltzer & Schroeder, *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems*, Proceedings of the IEEE, 1975 — least privilege is why a leaked secret should matter as little as possible.
- NIST SP 800-207, *Zero Trust Architecture*, 2020 — credential hygiene and short-lived tokens: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-207.pdf

# Category: data

## Soft Delete
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/data/soft-delete
- Category: data · Severity: advisory · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Delete in two phases — mark now, purge after the recovery window — so one bad click is reversible.
> Never issue a physical delete for business data in one step. Mark rows deleted with an audit trail (who, when, why), filter them out of queries by default, and purge for real only after a defined recovery window — with purge jobs that are themselves observable. When asked to delete something, confirm which of the two phases is actually wanted, and route irreversible purges through a human.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: advisory.**

## Definition

Soft delete splits deletion into two phases: an immediate, reversible logical delete (set a deleted_at timestamp, hide from queries) and a delayed, irreversible purge after a retention window. The recovery window converts one bad click, one buggy script, or one confused customer moment into an undo instead of an incident. Deletion stops being a single irreversible verb; it becomes a state transition with an audit trail, followed much later by a real removal.

## When to use

- User-generated content: accounts, posts, messages, files — anything a user can "delete" from a UI.
- Admin and moderation actions, where honest mistakes and abuse investigations overlap.
- Reference data with foreign-key dependents — hard-delete cascades are where schemas go to die.
- Anywhere the business needs an audit of deletions: who deleted what, when, and why.

## When NOT to use

- When law or contract defines a hard deletion deadline — the recovery window is capped by that deadline, not by comfort; right-to-erasure requests are the classic case.
- Security-sensitive values — a soft-deleted API key is still a credential; revoke and destroy immediately.
- High-volume ephemeral rows (sessions, cache entries) where two-phase machinery costs more than the data; use TTL expiry.
- Data you should never have kept: soft-deleting PII you had no right to retain is retention, not deletion.

## Anti-pattern

- The "Delete account" button wired directly to a hard DELETE with cascades.
- Soft delete without default query filtering — deleted rows resurface in every report until someone notices.
- Unique indexes that ignore the deleted state, so a deleted row blocks re-registration; use a partial unique index instead.
- Purge jobs nobody owns; the "temporary" deleted_at column quietly becomes permanent storage and a compliance liability.

## Code example

Wrong — irreversible, instant:

```python
def delete_account(user):
    db.run("DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ?", user.id)        # gone, instantly, for real
    db.run("DELETE FROM orders WHERE user_id = ?", user.id)  # cascade by hand, pray
```

Right — mark with audit, purge later:

```python
def delete_account(user, actor):
    # Phase 1: reversible mark + audit, applied instantly
    db.run("UPDATE users SET deleted_at = now(), deleted_by = ? WHERE id = ?",
           actor.id, user.id)
# Phase 2 (scheduled, after the 30-day window): purge in batches, with metrics per run
```

## Technical enforcement

The two phases are enforced by the database and the query layer, not by memory:

- **Query-layer default filter**: the ORM excludes deleted rows unless a query explicitly opts in; soft-deleted data is invisible to normal code paths.
- **Permission split**: application roles hold no hard-DELETE on soft-delete tables; only the purge job's dedicated role does, and only for rows past the window (see Least Authority).
- **Partial unique indexes**: uniqueness applies among live rows only, so deletion never blocks re-registration.
- **Purge as a first-class job**: batched, dry-runnable, metric-emitting, with alerts — deletion of deletions is still deletion (see Blast Radius).
- **Audit fields mandatory**: deleted_by, deleted_at, and reason are required columns; a deletion without provenance is a bug.

## Real-world case

(ilustratif) A customer, mid-way through a frustrating support ticket, deletes their account in another tab. The request is legitimate, the confirmation dialog is clicked through, and the workspace with all its files is hard-deleted before the agent reading the ticket ever sees it. With a 30-day soft-delete window, the account is restored in minutes and the support conversation continues; without one, the answer is "have you checked whether your data was important." (verification: perlu — the composite story is constructed; trash/undo windows are a common real product pattern, but this specific sequence is illustrative, belum digali.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Soft Delete vs. compliance**: retention windows must shrink to legal deadlines; when a regulation says gone, gone wins — track the tightest applicable deadline per data class.
- **Soft Delete vs. storage and liability**: deleted data that is never purged is a liability wearing a feature's clothes; the purge is part of the principle, not an optional extra.
- **Weigh against Blast Radius / user expectation**: a visible trash can and an explicit undo are honest UX; a hidden forever-deleted_at flag surprises users and engineers alike.

## Related principles

- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — the recovery window is a blast-radius cap in the time dimension.
- [Append-Only Logs](/docs/principles/data/append-only-logs) — deletion as an event in history rather than an edit of it.
- [Tested Backups](/docs/principles/data/tested-backups) — the last resort when the window has already closed.
- [Least Authority](/docs/principles/security/least-authority) — only the purge role may destroy, and only past the window.

## References

- Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2017 — log-structured storage and retention (verification: perlu — confirm framing before quoting).
- Privacy erasure regimes (e.g. the EU GDPR right to erasure) cap how long "deleted" may linger — check the exact obligations with counsel before writing retention policy (verification: perlu).

---

## Append-Only Logs
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/data/append-only-logs
- Category: data · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Record facts as appended events, never edited history — an append-only log is evidence and undo in one.
> Record state changes as appended, immutable events — with timestamp and actor — instead of editing rows in place. Never UPDATE or DELETE history: corrections are new events that supersede old ones, and physical removal happens only through an explicit, governed purge. Protect audit logs at the permission level so that no role, including yours, can quietly rewrite them.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

An append-only log records facts as events that are never edited or removed — the write-ahead log of databases and the event log of event sourcing, applied to business and audit data. Because history cannot be rewritten, the log is simultaneously evidence (who did what, in order) and recovery (state rebuilt by replaying events). Corrections are compensating events, not edits: the log shows the mistake and the fix, which is exactly what an investigation needs.

## When to use

- Audit trails: permission changes, payments, admin actions, access to sensitive data.
- State that must be reconstructible: event-sourced aggregates, materialized views rebuilt by replay.
- Integration between systems — the log is the durable interface; consumers read at their own pace and position.
- Multi-step workflows whose debugging requires the timeline, not just the current state.

## When NOT to use

- High-churn mutable state where event history would dwarf the state — keep the counter, log the anomalies.
- Simple CRUD where the current row is the whole truth; an event log adds machinery without adding answers.
- Data whose retention is legally bounded — append-only must pair with a governed purge path, or the log itself becomes the compliance problem.
- Hot-path reads: consumers query projections built from the log, never the raw log itself.

## Anti-pattern

- An audit table writable by the same application role, with UPDATE and DELETE granted alongside INSERT.
- "Fixing" history with an UPDATE — a rename that rewrites the actor column now lies about who did what.
- Events with client-supplied timestamps and no ordering guarantee.
- Treating the log as storage: querying it on every request instead of maintaining a projection.

## Code example

Wrong — history edited to taste:

```sql
-- "Fix" a wrong audit entry by editing it — history now lies
UPDATE audit_log SET action = 'refund:corrected', amount = 4200 WHERE id = 991;
DELETE FROM audit_log WHERE id = 992;   -- "that one was noise"
```

Right — corrections are new events; permissions enforce it:

```sql
-- Nothing before is ever edited or removed; the correction references the mistake
INSERT INTO audit_log (id, ts, actor, action, amount, supersedes)
VALUES (next_id(), now(), 'ops@corp', 'refund:corrected', 4200, 991);

-- DBA side, once: the database, not the code, is what actually enforces this
-- REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON audit_log FROM app_role;
```

## Technical enforcement

Immutability is a property of the store, not a promise of the code:

- **Database permissions**: application roles hold INSERT and SELECT on the log, never UPDATE or DELETE — revoke them and the point is enforced structurally (see Least Authority).
- **Write-once storage tiers** where available: object-lock buckets and WORM-like storage make rewriting impossible rather than forbidden.
- **Tamper evidence**: hash chaining or periodic anchoring of log digests makes tampering detectable, not just preventable.
- **Projections for reads**: consumers query derived views maintained from the log; the raw log is never on a hot path.
- **Governed purge**: removal from the log is itself a logged, approved event with its own audit trail — deletion must be visible in history.

## Real-world case

(ilustratif) An investigation into a suspicious funds transfer stalls because the audit table allowed UPDATE. A well-meaning cleanup script had "normalized" old entries years earlier; entries added later were corrected in place during a data-quality sprint. By the time investigators arrive, the table cannot distinguish a legitimate correction from tampering, and the reconstruction falls back to interviews and memory instead of data. Revoking UPDATE would have reduced the question "what happened?" from testimony to a query. (verification: perlu — the composite is constructed; real investigations blocked by mutable audit trails exist, belum digali — verify specific sources before citing any of them.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Append-Only vs. privacy and retention**: immutable logs of personal data collide with erasure duties — log the facts you must keep, hash or drop the PII you must not (weigh against Soft Delete).
- **Append-Only vs. queryability**: the log answers "what happened", a projection answers "what is" — you must maintain both, and reconcile them.
- **Weigh against KISS**: full event sourcing is an architecture; an append-only audit of critical actions is a table with revoked UPDATE — start there and stop until proven insufficient.

## Related principles

- [Soft Delete](/docs/principles/data/soft-delete) — deletion as an event rather than an edit of history.
- [Tested Backups](/docs/principles/data/tested-backups) — a replayable log is only real if replay has been rehearsed.
- [Least Authority](/docs/principles/security/least-authority) — the REVOKE is the principle, applied to history.
- [Idempotency](/docs/principles/reliability/idempotency) — stable event IDs make replay safe as well as possible.

## References

- Pat Helland, *Immutability Changes Everything*, CIDR 2015 — the case for immutable, append-only records (verification: perlu — confirm the exact paper and venue before quoting).
- Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2017 — write-ahead logs, log-structured storage, and event sourcing (verification: perlu).

---

## Tested Backups
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/data/tested-backups
- Category: data · Severity: critical · Status: draft · Verification: ok
- Summary: A backup without a tested restore is a hope, not a control — restore drills on schedule prove it works.
> Never claim data is backed up unless a restore from that backup has completed and its contents were verified. Schedule restore drills on real systems, measure recovery time and recovery point, and treat any backup that has never been restored as if it does not exist. Before any destructive operation, confirm with a human that the restore point is fresh and the restore path is known to work.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: critical.**

## Definition

A backup is only real after a successful restore test; everything else is a hope with a schedule. The restore path is the actual product: its recovery point objective (how much data you lose) and recovery time objective (how long you are down) are measured properties, not intentions. Drills on a cadence catch the silent rot — backups that stopped days ago, credentials that expired, formats that changed, restores that take far longer than anyone believes.

## When to use

- Any datastore whose loss is unacceptable: production databases, blob storage without re-derivable content, secrets vaults.
- Before destructive operations — mass deletions, schema migrations, manual surgery — verify the restore point first (see Blast Radius).
- After every backup-infrastructure change: new tool, new encryption, new storage location.
- Regimes where restore capability is audited (compliance, contracts, insurance).

## When NOT to use

- Data that can be fully re-derived — a rebuilt cache, a re-materialized dataset from source events; drill the re-derivation instead.
- Explicitly disposable environments; restoring sandboxes is theater.
- Never restore onto the live primary — the drill itself must not endanger production; restore into an isolated copy.

## Anti-pattern

- "We have backups" — unasked questions: when was the last one? Who has ever restored one? How long does it take?
- Backup job success monitored; restore never executed even once.
- Restores tested only in the first week after the tool was installed, two years ago.
- Backup credentials stored inside the system being backed up.
- Retention shorter than the time it takes to notice the corruption — you backed up the corrupted state.

## Code example

Wrong — dumps that nobody ever restores:

```bash
# Nightly cron dumps and uploads; success is assumed, never proven
pg_dump "$DATABASE_URL" | gzip | aws s3 cp - "s3://backups/db-$(date +%F).sql.gz"
```

Right — a scheduled drill that must pass:

```bash
# Restore the latest backup into an isolated database; time it — that is your RTO
aws s3 cp "s3://backups/$LATEST" - | gunzip | psql "$DRILL_DB_URL"
psql "$DRILL_DB_URL" -c "SELECT assert_fresh_data();"   # red build if data is stale
```

## Technical enforcement

If the restore is not scheduled and automated, it will not happen — make it a job:

- **Restore drill as a CI job**: on a schedule, restore the newest backup to an isolated environment and run data assertions; a red build means the backup is broken.
- **RTO and RPO as metrics**: every drill measures recovery time and data currency; drift over time is an incident, not a curiosity.
- **Alert on backup silence**: no successful backup event in N hours pages someone — silent skips, not just loud failures, are the killer.
- **Pre-destruction gate**: the ops tool requires a verified fresh restore point before a destructive run executes; this is enforced by the tool, not remembered by the operator.
- **Rehearsed runbooks with owners**: a full-environment restore game day at a fixed cadence, with a name attached.

## Real-world case

On 2017-01-31, a GitLab operator, exhausted after hours fighting replication problems, deleted the wrong directory on the primary database server — believing it held a secondary's data. The directory held the primary's live data. The team then discovered that of their five backup and replication mechanisms, most were unusable at that moment: broken, out of date, or unable to deliver recent data; the viable restore path was slower and less complete than expected, and six hours of user data (issues, merge requests, comments) were permanently lost. Postmortem: https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2017/02/01/gitlab-dotcom-database-incident/ — five mechanisms with zero rehearsed restores. A scheduled restore drill would have reduced the loss from six hours of permanent data loss to a bounded, known recovery point.

## Tension and trade-off

- **Tested Backups vs. cost**: drills consume storage, compute, and engineering time; treat the drill as the deliverable and the backup as its input.
- **Tested Backups vs. Soft Delete / Append-Only Logs**: backups are the last line of defense, not the first — layered recovery (event replay, soft delete, then restore) each reduces how far back the last resort reaches.
- **RPO vs. write latency**: more frequent backups or synchronous replication cost real write performance; decide per dataset with explicit numbers, not vibes.

## Related principles

- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — the fewer things one mistake can destroy, the less the backup matters.
- [Least Authority](/docs/principles/security/least-authority) — the operator who deleted the directory should not have had the authority to.
- [Append-Only Logs](/docs/principles/data/append-only-logs) — replayable history is a backup you use every day.
- [Soft Delete](/docs/principles/data/soft-delete) — reversible deletion for the mistakes that do not need the last resort.

## References

- GitLab, *GitLab.com Database Incident, 2017-01-31* — https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2017/02/01/gitlab-dotcom-database-incident/
- Google SRE Book — https://sre.google/sre-book/ (data integrity and emergency response practice; verify chapter pointers before citing them).

## Expand-Contract
- URL: https://principai.vercel.app/docs/principles/data/expand-contract
- Category: data · Severity: important · Status: draft · Verification: perlu
- Summary: Change schemas in compatible phases — add the new, migrate the data, then remove the old only when nothing reads it.
> Never deliver a schema or interface change in one breaking step. Add the new structure alongside the old, migrate data and readers gradually, and remove the old path only when usage telemetry proves nothing reads it — every intermediate state must survive with mixed versions running. If a migration would drop, rename, or repurpose something that other code may still read, stop and verify the consumers first.

*Instruction for AI agents — the operative rule.*

**Severity: important.**

## Definition

Expand-contract (parallel change) splits a breaking change into three compatible phases: expand (add the new structure without removing the old), migrate (backfill, dual-write, and switch readers over), and contract (remove the old only when usage telemetry shows zero readers). Every intermediate deploy must be safe to leave running for hours, because rollouts are gradual and rollback goes to old code, not forward.

## When to use

- Schema changes on tables with live traffic: add column, backfill, switch, then drop.
- Renaming or repurposing API fields — old and new fields served side by side across contract versions.
- Storage and message-format migrations with in-flight producers and consumers.
- Any system where deploy is not atomic and multiple app versions run simultaneously — which is the normal case.

## When NOT to use

- Pre-launch systems with no consumers and no data — migrate in one step and keep history trivial.
- Tables small enough to rebuild atomically inside one maintenance-window transaction with downtime already scheduled.
- When the old path is a security liability (leaking a secret, exposing private data) — plan a fast, explicit removal with compensations instead of a slow migration.

## Anti-pattern

- One migration, one deploy: DROP the old column and ADD the new one in the same release the app starts using it.
- Adding a NOT NULL column with a default to a hot table in the same deploy that writes it.
- Dual-write with no reconciliation job — the two paths drift silently and nobody notices.
- "Nothing reads the old field" verified by asking the loudest team, not by checking traffic.

## Code example

Wrong — one step, atomic in the worst sense:

```sql
-- Old code (still running during rollout) SELECTs legacy_total everywhere
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN legacy_total, ADD COLUMN total_cents BIGINT;
```

Right — three compatible phases:

```sql
-- Phase 1 (expand): additive only, nullable, no exclusive lock drama
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_cents BIGINT;

-- Phase 2 (migrate): backfill in batches; app dual-writes both and reconciles
UPDATE orders SET total_cents = legacy_total * 100
 WHERE total_cents IS NULL AND id % 64 = 0;

-- Phase 3 (contract): only after usage logs show zero reads of legacy_total
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN legacy_total;
```

## Technical enforcement

The phases are enforced by tooling that refuses to let humans compress them:

- **Migration linters in CI**: destructive DDL (DROP COLUMN, RENAME, type narrowing) cannot ship in the same release as the additive change; the split is mandatory.
- **Lock guards**: migrations run under lock and statement timeouts; a migration that would take a long exclusive lock on a hot table is rejected.
- **Usage telemetry before contract**: read counts per field and per consumer on dashboards; the drop is only allowed after zero for a full rollout cycle.
- **Reconciliation job**: while dual-writing, a scheduled diff between old and new paths alerts on drift — drift is a bug, not a tuning knob.
- **Decoupled deploy order**: migrations and app releases are separate pipelines with separate rollback plans.

## Real-world case

(ilustratif) A team ships the "cleanup" half of a rename migration on a Friday afternoon. Some app servers run the previous release for another hour; each one hits its first SELECT of the dropped column and fails every request it touches, and the rollback requires re-adding the column and re-running the backfill. The postmortem's first line: "we thought the deploy had finished." (verification: perlu — real drop-column incidents exist in public write-ups; belum digali — verify specific sources before citing any of them.)

## Tension and trade-off

- **Expand-Contract vs. speed**: three phases cost planning and coordination; a one-step migration is only acceptable when every reader is under your control and the table is cold.
- **Expand-Contract vs. clarity**: dual paths double schema and code surface; the contract phase is a commitment, not an option — schedule it, or the expansion becomes permanent debt.
- **Weigh against YAGNI / KISS**: for changes that are trivially backward compatible (additive, nullable, unused elsewhere), a straight migration is the simpler correct choice.

## Related principles

- [Hyrum's Law](/docs/principles/api/hyrum-law) — someone, somewhere, reads the old field; assume it and verify with telemetry.
- [Versioned Contracts](/docs/principles/api/versioned-contracts) — the API-facing form of the same phase discipline.
- [Fail-Visible](/docs/principles/reliability/fail-visible) — dual-write without reconciliation drifts silently in the direction of corruption.
- [Blast Radius](/docs/principles/reliability/blast-radius) — a bad migration phase should cost one batch, not the table.

## References

- Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2017 — schema evolution and encoding compatibility (verification: perlu — check the exact chapters before citing page numbers).
- Google SRE Workbook — https://sre.google/workbook/ (making production changes safely; verify chapter pointers).
